title: Railway Signalling for Technicians
text:
Start here
This book provides a starting point for learning about railway signalling. Begin with the Introduction for its purpose, intended readership and study guidance, then read the opening chapters in sequence.
Overview of a signalling scheme brings the main system relationships together. The equipment chapters develop those subjects, and Useful other sources of information provides references for further study.






ImportantAuthority for work



This is an educational introduction. It does not specify test limits, maintenance intervals, operating rules or authority to work. Use the applicable controlled documentation, local arrangements and competence requirements for work on the railway.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Who the book is for
This book is intended to be used as a starting point for those learning about railway signalling for the first time. It is designed to give a basic overview and understanding of signalling, and an introduction to the railway.
It is essentially my attempt at creating the book I wished I had when I first started.
The book is intended for those who are new to railway signalling, including those beginning work in signalling and telecommunications (S&T). It introduces the railway equipment, its purpose and the relationships between systems before moving into more detailed equipment descriptions.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 How to use the book
Read the opening chapters in sequence. Railway basics introduces line names, directions and location references. Railway signalling introduces train separation and control, while Overview of a signalling scheme brings the main equipment and system relationships together. The later chapters develop trackwork, points, signals, circuit reading, relays and the systems that connect them.
For each item, establish what it does, how it fits into the wider signalling system and what happens when it fails to perform its function.
Use Useful other sources of information to find references for further study. Practical work requires the applicable controlled documentation, local arrangements and competence; this introductory book does not define test limits, maintenance intervals or authority to work.

title: 2  Railway basics
text:
2.1 Responsibilities
Railway lines are formed of two running rails and sleepers between them. There are also various other components that you will see around the railway, some of which will belong to other departments. The track department, more commonly known as p-way, is responsible for looking after the track itself. This includes the rails, the sleepers, and the ballast.
Almost all of the railway surrounding Glasgow is now electrified using overhead lines. There are therefore overhead gantries and stantions dotted around to suspend the overhead lines from. The Overhead line department are responsible for looking after these, although the power is maintained by the Electrification and Plant (E&P) department. E&P are also responsible for switch heaters that run along the rails of points to keep them clear of snow and ice, and the compressed air which drives many of the points in Glasgow Central.
Off-track look after all the things which are not directly part of the railway, but are needed to keep it safe and secure. This includes fencing and vegetation. You might need to speak with them a lot in the summer months when trees begin to grow and obscure signals.
The Telecoms department are responsible for all the telecoms that is used by the railway. In years gone by this was part of the signalling department’s job, which is why we’re known as S&T, although now we do very little telecoms. The only telecoms we are still responsible for are signal post telephones (SPTs).

title: 2  Railway basics
text:
Background


The name “p-way” comes from the term “Permanent Way”, which was used to describe the final railway that was constructed. In the early days of railway building a “Temporary Way” was first quickly constructed to help get materials to site.

title: 2  Railway basics
text:
2.2 Tracks and lines
A track normally consists of two running rails and the structure that supports them. A single-track railway has one track; a double-track railway has two. A railway with four tracks has eight running rails. Points connect tracks so that trains can pass from one to another.
The word line often means a particular track, as in Up Main line. It can also describe a railway between places, so someone might say the Neilston line, but actually mean both the Up Neilston and the Down Neilston as they’re referring to the branch as a whole. A bit of context is often needed to know exactly which is being referred to.

title: 2  Railway basics
text:
2.3 Up and Down directions
Up and Down are established railway directions. They provide a consistent way to describe movements and distinguish tracks without relying on the direction in which someone happens to be looking. Up commonly means towards the principle station on that route, often the headquarters of the company which built that line. Many lines use London as the marker for the Up direction, but some lines in the area use Glasgow instead. This is just something that you will have to learn as you get to know the section.
Most lines will have one predominant direction of movement, so will be known as the Up or Down line. For example, the Up Fast mostly carries train in the Up direction, towards London. Some bits of it are bi-directionally signalled however, so trains can travel in either direction. This means it is possible for a train to be travelling in the Down direction (towards Glasgow) on the Up Fast.
Where there is a single-track section of railway these are normally bi-directionally signalled so that trains can travel in either direction. They will still have an Up and a Down direction though.

title: 2  Railway basics
text:
2.4 Line names
Fast and Slow are common line names, although in some regions the terms Main and Relief are more commonly used, with the same meanings. Fast lines are generally intended for faster or non-stopping services, with Slow lines more commonly associated with stopping passenger services or freight trains. Fast lines might have a higher maximum permissible speed than Slow lines, but this isn’t always the case. Often the line speed might actually be the same for both lines.
Lines may also have other designations, which might refer to geographical locations (e.g. Gourock or Hertford), usage (e.g. Suburban or Departure), or be named for historical reasons (e.g. City Union or Smithy Lye).  These designations are not necessarily an indication of how a line is used today, and their meaning may have been all but forgotten.

A number is used at the end of the ELR when there is a discontinuity in mileage along a route. This might happen if the track layout has changed over the years or the original measurements were very inaccurate.

Mileage
All lines also have a mileage, starting from a datum point. The origin points are normally the destination of the Up line, but there are some exceptions.

In Scotland mileages are given in Miles and Yards, but in the rest of the UK mileages are given in Miles and Chain. You might see chain used in some documents, such as the Sectional Appendix, so it’s important to know what this is.

title: 2  Railway basics
text:
2.6 The spaces around the track
The following names describe where something lies relative to the rails:







Term
Meaning




Four-foot
The space between the running rails of one track


Six-foot
The space between adjacent tracks in the usual double-track description


Ten-foot
The wider space between pairs of tracks in a four-track arrangement


Cess
The area alongside the outside of the running lines




These names identify spaces rather than certifying their dimensions, for example, four-foot is not the measurement used to specify track gauge. The Trackwork chapter explains gauge and the construction of the track.
You may also hear the 10-ft called a “wideway”.






Important



Spaces may be smaller than their names suggest. Do not rely on the names to judge whether you are in a position of safety.

title: 2  Railway basics
text:
2.7 How tracks appear on plans
A signalling scheme M12 plan generally represents each track by one line. That line stands for the complete track, not an individual rail. A double-track railway therefore appears as two lines even though it has four running rails. A detailed bonding diagram, by contrast, generally shows both rails as the individual connections between the rails matter.



Same junction on both an M12 signalling plan, a bonding diagram, and in real life


M12 diagrams are the most common diagram that you will come across. They show almost all signalling equipment, but can be confusing at first due to the number of symbols used. The above diagram contains the symbol for a point machine (the connected circle and rectangle).






Tip



Start by finding the orientation of a plan, using line names, stations, points, signals, or other features that are shown. It will become easier to relate what you see on the plan to what you see on the ground as you become more familiar with both the plans and the location.


It’s important to understand what is shown on each type of diagram so that you can relate it to the real world conditions on the ground.
Plans are generally to scale, but the scale may change throughout the plan depending on the complexity of the layout. Do not assume that just because two things look close together on the plan they will be a short walk in real life.
There is also an unofficial website [password: Glasg0w!] covering Glasgow showing the locations of all the assets and track circuits which can be useful when working out distances or finding assets. It’s vital to be able to understand official diagrams but this can be useful resource to assist you in getting to know the area.

title: 2  Railway basics
text:
2.8 Other diagrams
Another diagram you may come across are TAP diagrams. These can be found on the Scotland’s Railway Planning Hub. They can be a bit more user friendly, but aren’t used that often as they don’t give as much detail as an M12.





The Sectional Appendix is a document produced that gives all sorts of information about each lines, which is mostly relevant to train drivers. It does, however, include diagrams which contain some important information, such as line speeds and controlling signal box. The Sectional Appendix will always be included in your safe work pack and can also be found online.

title: 3  Railway signalling
text:
3.1 Safety and the service
The principal purpose of signalling is to organise movements so that trains do not collide. That includes a following train catching a train ahead, opposing trains meeting on the same line, and trains converging at a junction. Signalling also influences the service that can be operated. A railway carrying occasional trains has different capacity requirements from one carrying trains a few minutes apart.
These purposes are connected. Shortening the interval between trains requires a suitable method of separation and adequate warning for braking. Adding signals without considering braking, detection and route locking does not automatically create a useful increase in capacity.

title: 3  Railway signalling
text:
3.2 Why time alone is insufficient
A time-interval system releases a second train a specified time after the first. Its weakness is simple: the first train may have stopped. Elapsed time cannot prove that the line ahead is clear.
A space-interval system instead separates trains by defined sections. The key question becomes whether the preceding train has left the protected section. This is the foundation of block working. How the railway establishes that a section is available depends on the system and its associated operating arrangements.

title: 3  Railway signalling
text:
3.3 Absolute block
In a simple example, adjacent signal boxes A and B communicate using bells and block instruments. The receiving signaller controls indications associated with the section. The three indications are Line Blocked, Line Clear and Train on Line.
At a conceptual level, the receiving box agrees to accept a train, the sending box signals it forward under the required conditions, and the instruments record its entry into the section. The receiving box establishes that the train has arrived complete before the section is made available again. Arrival of the locomotive alone is insufficient: vehicles could have become detached and remain in the section.
This explanation identifies the safety purpose of the communications. It is not a bell-code sequence or an instruction for operating block instruments.






ImportantTwo different protections



Block working organises the separation of trains along a line. Interlocking prevents incompatible settings and movements within its designed scope. A junction can be correctly set while the line ahead is occupied; an empty line does not prove that a junction is correctly set.

title: 3  Railway signalling
text:
3.4 Electrical operation and control
A point machine provides the force at the points, while electrical detection reports the required resulting conditions. Relay circuits or electronic interlockings enforce the movement constraints, allowing the control interface and the equipment implementing the safety logic to have different physical forms. The operator’s command, the equipment action and the resulting indication are separate parts of the system.

title: 3  Railway signalling
section: 3.5 Track circuit block and automatic signals
text:
3.5 Track circuit block and automatic signals
A track circuit uses the rails as part of an electrical circuit to establish whether a defined section is clear. It gives the signalling system information that does not depend on the signaller remembering the position of every train.
With continuous train detection and suitable controls, a plain-line signal can respond automatically to conditions ahead. In track circuit block, train detection supports the separation of trains between signals. Automatic describes how a signal is controlled; it does not mean that it operates without safety conditions.
The signal aspects must give the driver the required warning of a stop indication. The lineside signals chapter connects that requirement to braking distance, overlaps and headway.

title: 3  Railway signalling
section: 3.6 From individual controls to route setting
text:
3.6 From individual controls to route setting
With individual controls, the signaller sets the points and then operates the signal control. An entrance-exit (NX) interface lets the signaller identify the start and end of the required movement. The system calls the required points and establishes the route conditions.
The route command does not override the interlocking. If a required point is not detected, a track section is occupied or a conflicting route remains locked, the commanded proceed aspect cannot be obtained under those conditions.
Remote control makes it possible to operate geographically separated interlockings from a signalling centre without providing a separate long-distance wire for every control and indication. The interlocking and remote control system perform different jobs, a distinction developed later in the course.

title: 3  Railway signalling
text:
3.7 Train describers: background
A train describer associates a service identity with a displayed position, or berth, and uses train-detection and route information to step the description as the train moves. Its information can also support passenger displays and other operational systems. It identifies the service associated with a position; it does not prove the track clear or replace the interlocking’s safety checks. A wrong description can therefore cause confusion or misrouting even when the interlocking continues to prevent conflicting movements.

title: 3  Railway signalling
text:
3.8 Automatic Warning System
The Automatic Warning System (AWS) provides an audible indication in the cab. A warning requires acknowledgement by the driver; if it is not acknowledged, the system initiates a brake application.
AWS supports the driver by drawing attention to a warning. It works alongside the signals and the driver’s knowledge of the route.

title: 3  Railway signalling
section: 3.9 Activity: two trains at a junction
text:
3.9 Activity: two trains at a junction
Train A is standing beyond a junction. Train B is approaching a signal before it. The points are correctly set for B’s intended route. Explain why that fact alone cannot justify clearing B’s signal.






NoteSuggested reasoning





Correct point position establishes only one condition. The line to be used must also satisfy the train-detection and separation requirements, the required overlap and protection must be available, and conflicting movements must be excluded. A train standing beyond the junction may prevent these conditions being met.

title: 3  Railway signalling
text:
3.10 Key points

Time elapsed does not prove that a train has cleared a section.
Block working and interlocking address related but distinct problems.
Route setting simplifies entering commands; the interlocking still governs the result.
AWS draws attention to a warning and requires the driver to acknowledge it.

title: 4  Overview of a signalling scheme
text:
4.1 The system as a whole
A railway moves vehicles along a guided path. A train cannot steer round an obstruction and may need a substantial distance to stop. Signalling organises movements so that the required route and separation are established before the train proceeds.
Track provides the path, points select it, train detection reports occupation, and the interlocking determines when a movement may be authorised. Signals communicate the permitted movement to the driver. Power supplies and telecommunications support those functions.
A useful first drawing separates the control device, interlocking and railway equipment. Commands travel towards the equipment; indications return information about its state.
The arrows are functional relationships, not a statement that every installation uses a separate cable for each arrow. Relay interlockings and SSI implement the relationships differently.

title: 4  Overview of a signalling scheme
text:
4.2 Command, action and indication
Follow the command, action and indication separately. The command tells the equipment what to do; the action is what the equipment does; the indication reports its state. A command can be registered without the equipment completing its movement, so an indication must be understood through the equipment and circuit arrangement.
The signaller uses a control panel or workstation to enter commands and view indications. A track layout and equipment indications may share the same screen, but their physical combination does not make their engineering functions identical.
The interlocking checks the designed conditions and controls the railway equipment accordingly. It receives information such as point detection, train-detection states and signal proving. The signaller’s command passes through this logic before it can result in a permitted movement.
crumbs: 4  Overview of a signalling scheme

title: 4  Overview of a signalling scheme
section: 4.3 Follow a movement through the system
text:
4.3 Follow a movement through the system
Imagine a train waiting at a signal before a junction. The signaller wants it to take the branch. Several distinct events must occur:

The signaller enters a route command.
The interlocking checks the conditions associated with that route.
Points are called to the required positions where movement is permitted.
Detection reports the positions and locking conditions required by the design.
The interlocking establishes that the necessary conditions are proved and that conflicting movements are excluded.
The signal can display the permitted aspect.
Train detection reports the train’s progress, supporting the designed release of the route.

This sequence is simplified. Each stage depends on the actual equipment and controls: registering the command, supplying the operating energy, completing the action and obtaining the relevant indications are separate events.
crumbs: 4  Overview of a signalling scheme

title: 4  Overview of a signalling scheme
text:
4.4 Fail-safe behaviour
A right-side failure produces a more restrictive result than the traffic conditions require. For example, loss of a track-clear proving circuit may prevent a signal clearing even though the track is physically empty. A wrong-side failure produces a less restrictive result than the conditions justify, such as an occupied section being indicated clear to the safety logic.
Fail-safe design aims to prevent specified faults from producing unsafe permissions. It does not mean that equipment cannot fail, nor that every possible failure automatically lights a red lamp. A failed power supply can leave a signal dark. The safety arrangement must address the loss of the required information or indication as part of the design and operating system.






ImportantThink in terms of permission



The central question is whether the failure can allow a movement that should be prevented. “A fault has occurred” does not by itself tell you whether its effect is right-side or wrong-side.

title: 4  Overview of a signalling scheme
section: 4.5 Power is a separate engineering path
text:
4.5 Power is a separate engineering path
The logic deciding that points may move does not supply the mechanical energy needed to move them. Similarly, a command for a signal aspect does not itself supply the lamp’s energy. Power supplies, distribution cables, transformers, rectifiers and local protection support the control system.
A signalling-centre power cubicle provides supplies at the required voltages, trackside distribution and standby arrangements. One arrangement uses 650 V distribution to trackside equipment, with local conversion to the required working supplies. Individual circuits in a location case operate at their specified voltages.
A common supply can affect several apparently unrelated items. When several indications disappear together, their shared power or communications path is a relevant system relationship to examine in the drawings.
crumbs: 4  Overview of a signalling scheme

title: 4  Overview of a signalling scheme
text:
4.6 Cable routes and equipment housings
Cables follow a planned route, often in troughing. Undertrack crossings carry routes between sides of the railway. The route protects and organises cables; it also brings the signalling system into contact with civil-engineering work, drainage and the track environment.
A location case, often called a loc, houses interfaces close to the equipment. It can contain terminals, relays, track-circuit apparatus, local supplies and other equipment appropriate to the installation. Short connections from a housing to the signal, point equipment or rails are commonly called tail cables.
An equipment room provides more space where a group of cases would be unsuitable. The important relationship is the same: equipment housings provide the interface between the wider scheme and local railway assets.
crumbs: 4  Overview of a signalling scheme

title: 4  Overview of a signalling scheme
text:
4.7 Automatic route setting and telecommunications
Automatic route setting can add a further layer of commands using timetable and train information. The commands remain subject to interlocking conditions.
Telecommunications provides both human communications and data paths. Signal post telephones, point-area telephones and radio are examples. A transmission network can also carry remote control and other operational information. The service being carried and the physical bearer carrying it should be considered separately.
crumbs: 4  Overview of a signalling scheme

title: 4  Overview of a signalling scheme
text:
4.8 Other interfaces
Level crossings and the Automatic Warning System (AWS) connect signalling with other parts of the railway. Each has a different purpose:







Interface
Main purpose




Level crossing equipment
Manage the interface between road and rail movements


AWS
Provide an in-cab warning or clear indication associated with an approach



These interfaces are introduced here to explain their place in the signalling system. Equipment-specific chapters can develop their operation in more detail.

title: 4  Overview of a signalling scheme
section: 4.9 Worked example: one symptom, several paths
text:
4.9 Worked example: one symptom, several paths
A display shows that a branch route command has been registered and the points have been commanded reverse, but the entry signal remains at danger. Someone concludes that the signal must have failed because the command went through.
Registration of the command does not establish that the points moved, the required detection was obtained or every signal control condition was satisfied. Follow the system relationships:

Command: was the intended route or point command registered?
Energy: was the required supply available to the equipment?
Action and indication: did the equipment move and lock, and was the required detection indication obtained?
Signal controls: were all other conditions for clearing the signal satisfied?

A signal remaining at danger may be the correct response to a missing indication elsewhere. This example organises the evidence; it does not prescribe an order for intrusive tests or identify a failed component from the final symptom alone.

title: 4  Overview of a signalling scheme
text:
4.10 Key points

Command, action and indication are distinct parts of the equipment sequence.
A registered command does not establish that every subsequent stage has completed.
The interlocking separates the movement command from the permission to act.
Power, communications and physical railway equipment are all part of the scheme.
Failure classification depends on the safety consequence.
An interface drawing is a useful starting point for understanding a whole installation.

title: 5  Trackwork
text:
5.1 The track is part of the signalling environment
Track provides a load-bearing, guided path for the train. For S&T, it can also be part of an electrical circuit, a support for detection equipment and a mechanical reference for point operation. Changes to track geometry, rail joints or support can therefore affect signalling equipment.
A simple track assembly consists of two rails held at the required gauge by sleepers and fastenings. Ballast supports the sleepers, distributes load and helps restrain the track while allowing drainage and resilience. Other forms use a concrete slab or embedded support rather than a conventional ballast bed.

title: 5  Trackwork
text:
5.2 Rails and fastenings
Two rail forms are bullhead and flat-bottom rail. Bullhead rail has a relatively narrow base and is held in chairs, traditionally by keys. Flat-bottom rail has a broad foot and uses suitable baseplates or direct fastenings, including spring clips.
Rail section designations can include a mass per unit length. Keep the units attached to the number: a designation expressed in kilograms per metre cannot be compared numerically with one expressed in pounds per yard without conversion. UIC 54 and BS110A illustrate the distinction between metric and imperial rail designations.
Sleepers may be timber, concrete or steel. Their purpose is more than carrying the rail vertically: they maintain the relationship between the rails and transfer lateral and longitudinal forces into the supporting structure. Electrical insulation within the fastening arrangement can be essential where the rails form a track circuit.

title: 5  Trackwork
text:
5.3 Ballasted and slab track
Ballast must support the sleepers firmly without making the track a completely rigid structure. Tamping consolidates the ballast under and around sleepers. Trackside cables, rail connections and point equipment occupy some of the same working area, so track maintenance has important S&T interfaces.
Slab and embedded track use different support arrangements. One tunnel arrangement places concrete support blocks in resilient boots, allowing the support to accommodate traffic loads without behaving as an unyielding mass. The underlying lesson is that a track assembly needs controlled geometry and suitable resilience, whatever its form.






NoteIn practice



When looking at a signalling item fixed to the railway, identify what holds it in its intended position. A detector attached to a rail, a machine mounted beside points and a cable fixed to a sleeper have different mechanical reference points and different exposure to track work.

title: 5  Trackwork
section: 5.4 Rail joints and continuous welded rail
text:
5.4 Rail joints and continuous welded rail
Fishplates join rail ends mechanically. A conventional joint creates a discontinuity that must be maintained. Welding reduces the number of joints and changes how thermal expansion is managed within the track structure.
Temperature changes still matter in welded rail. Expansion and contraction are restrained, so longitudinal forces develop. Track design, stressing and maintenance govern those forces. The applicable stressing requirements must be established for the site.
For signalling, the electrical function of a joint is a separate question from its mechanical function. An ordinary joint may need a bond to provide a dependable electrical path. An insulated rail joint intentionally interrupts that path. A glued insulated joint combines mechanical strength with electrical separation and can be incorporated into welded track.
The question to ask is therefore not simply “is there a joint?” but “what continuity or insulation is intended here?” The train-detection chapter develops the consequences.

title: 5  Trackwork
text:
5.5 Gauge and the wheel-rail interface
Track gauge is the distance between the specified inner faces of the rails. Standard gauge is 1,435 mm. It is distinct from loading gauge, which concerns the space available for a vehicle and its load.
A wheelset has two wheels connected by an axle. The wheel treads are profiled rather than being simple cylindrical surfaces. A lateral displacement changes the effective rolling radii at the contacts, contributing to guidance. Flanges provide an important boundary to movement, but ordinary guidance cannot be explained merely as flanges continuously rubbing against the rails.
At points and crossings the wheel-rail relationship becomes more complex because routes diverge and flangeways interrupt parts of the running surface. This is why the next chapter introduces check rails and crossings as well as moving point blades.

title: 5  Trackwork
section: 5.6 Relating the track to its plan
text:
5.6 Relating the track to its plan
Railway basics explains how tracks are represented on plans, how lines are named and how the spaces around them are described. Use those references to identify the track before considering its construction or the equipment attached to it.

title: 5  Trackwork
section: 5.7 Activity: a joint has two jobs
text:
5.7 Activity: a joint has two jobs
A rail joint is mechanically sound, but its insulating components no longer provide the intended electrical separation. Explain why a satisfactory mechanical inspection alone cannot establish that the signalling arrangement is correct.






NoteSuggested reasoning





The joint supports and connects the rail ends mechanically, but its signalling purpose may be to separate adjacent track circuits. Losing insulation can connect circuits that should be electrically separated. Mechanical condition and electrical function must both be understood.

title: 5  Trackwork
text:
5.8 Key points

Track supports and guides the vehicle and can form part of signalling circuits.
Mechanical continuity and electrical continuity are different requirements.
Track geometry and support affect equipment attached to the railway.
Track gauge and wheel profiles govern the wheel–rail relationship.

title: 6  Points
text:
6.1 Selecting a physical path
Points allow one track to divide into two, or two tracks to converge into one. The fixed outside rails are stock rails. The moving rails are switch blades, also called point blades. The moving end is the toe. Moving the blades closes one against its stock rail while opening the other to provide a flangeway.
Stretcher arrangements maintain the required relationship between the blades. Beyond them, the crossing provides the intersection of the rail paths. A fixed crossing includes gaps needed for wheel flanges. Check rails guide the wheelset through this area by acting against the back of a wheel flange, helping the opposite wheel follow the intended path at the crossing nose.
A turnout is therefore a coordinated assembly of moving and fixed track components. The machine is only one part of it.

title: 6  Points
text:
6.2 Rail form and switch fit
The stock rail can be bullhead or flat-bottom and can have an inclined or vertical arrangement. Switch-rail profiles include undercut, straight-cut and chamfered forms. The mounting and fittings must suit the actual rail and switch combination.
Where the stock rail is inclined, the switch rail need not have the same inclination. Looking only at the visible head or assuming that every turnout has the same section can therefore give an incorrect picture of blade fit and detector geometry.
Closure concerns the relationship of the closed switch to its stock rail. Opening concerns the space provided between the opposite switch and stock rail for the wheel flange. Both matter. A blade that is held clear at its toe does not automatically establish the correct shape and clearance over its whole working length.

title: 6  Points
text:
6.3 Two independent descriptions
Normal and reverse identify the two designated positions of the points. The designation is recorded on the plan. Normal must not be inferred merely because a route looks straight or appears to carry more traffic.
Facing and trailing describe the direction of a movement relative to the turnout. A facing movement approaches the toes and encounters the divergence. A trailing movement approaches from one of the converging tracks.

title: 6  Points
text:
6.4 Crossovers, diamonds and slips
A crossover combines two point ends to connect adjacent tracks. The two ends may be operated under one identity. Their detection must establish the conditions required for the combined movement; seeing one end correctly positioned does not establish the state of the other.
A diamond crossing lets two tracks cross at the same level without providing a route from one into the other. A switch diamond replaces parts of the fixed crossing arrangement with moving rails. A single slip adds a connection around one side of a diamond; a double slip provides connections around both sides. A scissors crossover combines crossovers within a compact length and includes a crossing between them.
A swing-nose crossing uses a movable crossing nose to close the required running path. Where moving crossings are provided, the blades and crossing equipment must be correctly coordinated and proved for the route.
The learning task is to trace each possible path before counting point machines. Complex trackwork may have several moving parts serving one movement.

title: 6  Points
text:
6.5 Catch points and trap points
Spring catch points are intended to derail vehicles running back down a gradient. Trap points protect a running line against an uncontrolled movement from a siding or other connected line.
A trap arrangement provides protection by directing an unauthorised movement away from the line being protected. The derailing position can be its designated normal position. The fact that it leads away from usable track does not make it a mistaken setting.
These arrangements show that the safety purpose of a set of points may include protection from a movement as well as routing an authorised one.

title: 6  Points
text:
6.6 Drive, lock and detect
Power-operated points have three functions that must be distinguished:







Function
Purpose




Drive
Supply and transmit the force to move the blades


Lock
Restrain the required parts in their established position


Detect
Provide the electrical evidence required by the interlocking



In a typical electric point machine, a motor drives gearing and a mechanism that converts rotary motion into linear movement. A clutch limits the consequences of an obstruction. A lock mechanism follows a sequence of unlocking, moving and relocking. Separate detector connections follow the blades and operate the detection contacts.
The machine arrangement described here has four mechanical connections: one drive, one lock and a detector connection for each blade. They do different jobs. Motor rotation or completion of part of the drive stroke is not enough to prove that the whole turnout has reached the required state.
The mechanical reference is also important. If detection depends on the relationship between blades and a machine, the mounting and connection between the machine, rails and track support are part of the complete arrangement.






ImportantDetection is evidence with a defined meaning



A detection circuit is intended to prove specified mechanical conditions. Its validity depends on the complete arrangement, including its adjustment, connections and reference points. An indication is not a substitute for understanding those conditions.

title: 6  Points
text:
6.7 Methods of operation

Combined and non-combined electric machines
A combined machine brings the drive, locking and detection mechanisms into the machine assembly. External connections associate those mechanisms with the switch rails and stretcher arrangements.
A non-combined machine provides the movement while the lock and detector are separate items. In an SGE HA arrangement, separate operating connections drive the switches and a remote facing point lock, with a separate detector following the required conditions.
The distinction is about where the functions are implemented. Non-combined does not mean that the turnout can dispense with locking or detection. It means the complete equipment layout must be followed beyond the motor housing.

title: 6  Points
text:
6.8 HW machines
An HW mechanism uses a motor, gearing and a bevel gear to operate a throw bar through an escapement. A roller moving in the shaped escapement slot produces phases in which the lock mechanism moves while the throw bar remains stationary, followed by the movement of the switches.
The sequence has three functional stages:

Unlock: the mechanism withdraws the lock dog from the established lock notch.
Drive: the throw bar transfers the switch rails to the opposite lie.
Relock and prove: the lock dog enters the other notch and the detector mechanism establishes the specified final conditions.

Lock blades follow the lock connection, while detector blades follow the switches through their individual rods. Their final relationship is what allows the detection contacts to provide the required detection indication. The motor reaching a particular rotation cannot substitute for that relationship.
The HW 1000 and HW 2000 arrangements have different motor and clutch designs. The HW 1000 uses a split-field motor with a friction clutch in the arrangement described here; the HW 2000 uses a permanent-magnet motor and electromagnetic clutch. The clutch limits transmitted torque when movement is obstructed, but correct functioning still depends on the specified control and protection.

title: 6  Points
text:
6.9 Electro-pneumatic points
An electro-pneumatic (EP) machine obtains its operating force from compressed air. Electrical valves control that force. Loss of electrical control and loss of air pressure can therefore produce similar final symptoms through different paths.
A typical SGE arrangement includes an air motor, valve unit, escapement mechanism and detector. The air motor is a piston and cylinder. Applying pressure to one side while exhausting the other produces the required direction of movement.
The electrical needle valves provide the normal, reverse and lock-control functions. They operate control-air paths which in turn operate the main air valves. This lets relatively small electrical devices control the larger air flow needed by the motor.
In the normal sequence, the direction is selected and the lock-control function enables the air supply. The escapement coordinates unlocking, switch movement and relocking. When the required final conditions are detected, the operating pressure is removed and the cylinder is exhausted as designed. Mechanical locking preserves the established position; continuous air force is not a substitute for the lock.
A separate point detector follows both switch rails and the lock slide in the arrangement described. The supply reservoir, pipes, valves, piston, mechanism and detection connections are all relevant to an account of the movement.

Worked example: valves called, no final detection
An EP direction command and lock command are registered, but the points do not reach valid detection. Several explanations remain possible: insufficient air supply, failure to admit or exhaust air, resistance in the mechanism, incomplete blade movement or a missing detection indication. The commands alone cannot distinguish them.
The useful study exercise is to follow electrical command → valve action → air flow → piston movement → escapement and switch movement → locking and detection. A missing final indication does not identify the detector as the only possible source of the failure.

title: 6  Points
text:
6.10 Clamp locks
A clamp lock arrangement uses hydraulic power to move drive-lock slides. The sequence first unlocks the closed blade, then transfers the blades, then clamps the newly closed blade to its stock rail. Detection is associated with the rail-mounted mechanism and includes conditions for both the closed and open blade.
This gives another implementation of the same functional sequence. It also shows why mechanical support, rail attachment and electrical insulation are important interfaces between permanent way and S&T.
The introductory comparison concerns operating principles. Product-specific adjustment values, motor run times, manual operation and tests belong in the relevant controlled equipment documentation.

Components of the clamp-lock arrangement
A rail clamp-lock installation has a lock-and-detector mechanism associated with each side, drive-lock slides, actuators, a coupling arrangement and an electro-hydraulic power pack. The lock body references the stock rail, while the switch carries the parts that move with it.
The power pack drives the selected hydraulic actuator while allowing fluid from the opposite side to return. Initial slide movement releases the closed switch’s lock arm. Continued movement transfers the switches. Final movement raises and supports the newly closed side’s lock arm so that the blade is clamped and the required detection can be established.
The stretcher and coupling arrangements have distinct roles. In the mechanism described, the stretcher transfers the other switch while the coupling coordinates the drive-lock slides and the retracting actuator. Calling every connecting bar a drive rod obscures that sequence.
Track movement can change the relationships on which the mechanism depends. Road spread concerns a change in the relationship between the stock rails; switch creep is longitudinal movement of the switch relative to its reference position. Rail attachments and the permanent-way condition therefore contribute to the equipment’s performance.

title: 6  Points
text:
6.11 Back drives and supplementary detection
A long switch requires controlled movement beyond the toe. A back drive transmits or supplies movement farther along the switch so that the closed rail fits and the open rail provides the required clearance over its working length.
Mechanical back drives use rods, cranks and supported connections. Hydraulic arrangements use additional actuators associated with the power pack. The number and positions depend on the turnout design; they cannot be inferred from the toe machine alone.
Supplementary detectors can provide detection indications farther along the switch. Toe detection and a back drive perform different functions: one reports defined conditions at its connection, while the other controls movement elsewhere. A satisfactory toe indication cannot automatically establish every condition along a long switch.

title: 6  Points
text:
6.12 Insulating the point fittings
A metal stretcher or sole plate can create an unwanted electrical connection between rail paths. Insulation within the fittings preserves the separation needed by the track circuit while retaining the mechanical connection.
Insulated arrangements can include divided sole plates and stretchers, bushes, ferrules, washers and insulation pieces at rods or fittings. An insulated ferrule separates the bolt from the surrounding metal; an insulating washer separates faces. Replacing only one part of that separation can leave another conductive path.
The required points include the switch and lock connections, detector rods and drive connections appropriate to the layout. A mechanically secure repair can still be electrically wrong if its insulation is defeated. Relate the fittings to the bonding arrangement as well as to the point machine.

title: 6  Points
section: 6.13 What lock and detection tests establish
text:
6.13 What lock and detection tests establish
A facing point lock test establishes the specified relationship between switch fit and lock engagement. A detection test establishes the required relationship between the actual switch and lock conditions and the electrical indication. They address different links in the chain.
Testing has both safety and reliability purposes. The detection must not indicate the required position outside its permitted mechanical conditions, while the equipment must operate reliably within its permitted working tolerance. Setting everything as tight as possible can produce unreliable operation or mask the intended sequence.
The test positions, gauges, preparation and acceptance values depend on the mechanism and applicable specification. A point machine and a rail clamp lock do not necessarily use the same means of separating lock indication from switch detection during a test. Those procedures must be learnt from the equipment-specific instructions and carried out under the required authority.

title: 6  Points
text:
6.14 Worked example: one end detected
A crossover is commanded reverse. End A is reported reverse, but end B has no valid detection. Can the signal clear simply because the first end is correct?
No. The route depends on a continuous, correctly established path through both ends. If the required detection includes both ends, the interlocking is missing part of its evidence. A successful drive command and one end’s indication cannot stand in for the other end’s indication.

title: 6  Points
text:
6.15 Key points

Normal/reverse are designated positions; facing/trailing describe movements.
Points and crossings include fixed rails, moving rails and guidance through crossings.
Drive, locking and detection are separate but coordinated functions.
Combined, non-combined, EP and hydraulic equipment implement those functions in different arrangements.
Back drives and supplementary detection address conditions beyond the switch toe.
Trap points protect a line from an unwanted movement.
The mechanical reference and electrical insulation form part of the signalling arrangement.

title: 7  Lineside signals
text:
7.1 Communicating with the driver
An aspect is the indication displayed by a signal. Colour-light signals distinguish aspects by colours or combinations of colours. Position-light signals also use the arrangement of the lights. The meaning must be taken from the applicable signalling system, rather than from colour alone.
In route signalling, signals communicate movement information and route indications identify a divergence or destination. The driver also needs knowledge of the route and its speed restrictions. This differs from systems that use aspects to communicate specified speed categories directly.
A signal at its most restrictive aspect is said to be on. When it displays a less restrictive aspect it is off, or has cleared. Clearing does not necessarily mean displaying green: a signal displaying yellow has also cleared from red.

title: 7  Lineside signals
text:
7.2 Warning before a stop
A sequence of red/green stop signals needs an associated means of warning the driver about a red signal early enough to stop. Yellow/green distant or repeater signals can provide this warning in association with the stop signals.
The governing relationship is between the point at which the driver receives the warning and the location where the train must stop. Braking requirements depend on the trains and the railway, including gradient. Visibility of the red signal alone may not provide sufficient stopping distance.
A three-aspect system combines stop and warning functions at successive signals:







Aspect in the simplified sequence
Information conveyed




Red
Stop


Single yellow
Be prepared to stop at the next signal


Green
The next signal is displaying a proceed aspect within this sequence



A four-aspect system adds double yellow as an earlier caution in the sequence. A simplified progression towards a signal at red is green, double yellow, single yellow, red.






Figure 7.1: A simplified four-aspect warning sequence, read in the direction of travel. Actual spacing and controls depend on the design.



This is a principle diagram. It does not cover flashing aspects, special sequences or every possible installation.

title: 7  Lineside signals
text:
7.3 Overlaps
An overlap provides a defined distance beyond a stop signal as part of the protection for a train approaching that signal. In a simple plain-line arrangement, the signal in rear requires the appropriate section and overlap beyond the next stop signal to be clear.
The overlap is additional protection for an overrun; it is not an extension of the driver’s authority to pass the stop signal. It can include points and more than one train-detection section. Those conditions must be dealt with by the interlocking.

title: 7  Lineside signals
text:
7.4 Headway
Headway is the separation between successive trains, expressed as a distance or as a time at a stated speed. A minimum-distance headway calculation must include the stated assumptions, such as train length, overlap, signal sighting allowance and braking distance.
For a simplified, evenly spaced plain-line arrangement:
\[H_3 = L + O + 2B + S\]
\[H_4 = L + O + 1.5B + S\]
Here \(H_3\) and \(H_4\) are the three- and four-aspect headway distances, \(L\) is train length, \(O\) is overlap length, \(B\) is braking distance and \(S\) is a sighting allowance, all expressed in the same distance unit. These simplified teaching relationships depend on the stated assumptions; they are not general design rules for all layouts.
For an invented example, take \(L = 200\) m, \(O = 180\) m, \(B = 1{,}000\) m and \(S = 200\) m. The results are \(H_3 = 2{,}580\) m and \(H_4 = 2{,}080\) m. At a constant 20 m/s, these distances correspond to 129 s and 104 s respectively. The reduction is 500 m, or 25 s at that speed. Actual service planning also depends on junctions, station stops, varying speeds and other constraints.
Adding intermediate signals does not halve every component of headway. Train length, overlap and sighting allowance remain in this simplified comparison.

title: 7  Lineside signals
text:
7.5 Inside a filament colour-light signal
In a separate-aperture filament signal, each aspect has a compartment containing its lamp, holder, electrical connections and optical system. Internal partitions prevent an illuminated lamp from lighting the lens of another aspect. The rear access and sealing arrangements protect these relationships from dirt, water and disturbance.
A double-filament lamp has a main and auxiliary filament with the required contacts and common connection. The holder fixes their position relative to the optical system. The correct lamp type and orientation matter: two lamps with similar bases can have different filament geometry or ratings.
The optical assembly collects and directs the light into the required beam. A long-range lens concentrates the light; a spread arrangement provides a wider viewing field where required. A hot strip directs part of the light towards the position of a driver close to the signal. Beam alignment is therefore more than pointing the outside of the housing towards the track.
Hoods, backgrounds and control of reflections support recognition of the intended aspect. A phantom aspect is an apparent illumination caused by extraneous light, such as sunlight, rather than the intended lamp. Maintaining sighting and optical integrity preserves the meaning of the electrical control.

The electrical supply to the lamp
A filament arrangement can send an a.c. supply along the tail cable and step it down at an aspect transformer in the signal head. This reduces the current required in the longer cable compared with distributing the same power at the lower lamp voltage. The transformer and lamp connections still have to provide the specified conditions at the filament.
Separate tappings or connections can set the intended main and auxiliary operation. The lamp’s nominal marking is not necessarily the specified operating value in the complete assembly. Adjustments, beam setting and holder position are governed by the applicable equipment instructions.

title: 7  Lineside signals
section: 7.6 Aspect selection, filament changeover and lamp proving
text:
7.6 Aspect selection, filament changeover and lamp proving

Lamp proving

In a simplified four-aspect relay arrangement, the following states produce the normal sequence:

The control logic enforces the intended progression. It does not normally allow an arbitrary combination such as DR up with HR down. These names and states explain the particular arrangement; other signal technologies implement the functions differently.
A local lamp relay can be energised by the main-filament current. If that filament opens, the relay releases and switches the supply to the auxiliary filament. Monitoring can report that the main filament has failed even though the signal remains illuminated.
The ECR lamp-proving function provides separate evidence used by the signalling controls. Its slow-release characteristic can bridge the short interruption during a legitimate aspect change or filament changeover, while a sustained loss removes the corresponding lamp-proving indication. The specified delay and proving path are part of the circuit design.
In the four-aspect arrangement described, the second yellow has a different proving treatment from the red, first yellow and green. Losing only the second yellow changes double yellow to the more restrictive single yellow. That example should not be extended to every multi-lamp display: some missing lamps can make a route indication ambiguous rather than simply more restrictive.

Worked example: a lamp is lit but a filament alarm remains
A signal continues to display its selected aspect after its main filament fails. The auxiliary is carrying the required current, but a filament alarm is present. These observations can be consistent: changeover has preserved the display while monitoring reports the loss of the main filament.
The alarm and lamp-proving functions answer different questions. A visible light does not prove that both filaments are intact, while a main-filament alarm does not necessarily mean that the signal is dark. Read the particular lamp and proving circuit before interpreting either indication.

title: 7  Lineside signals
text:
7.7 Searchlight signals
A searchlight signal uses a lamp and an optical path with a moving coloured roundel. Its mechanism selects red, yellow or green within that path. In the arrangement considered here, the released mechanism selects red; energisation with one polarity selects yellow and the opposite polarity selects green.
Mechanism contacts repeat the roundel’s position. Lamp-current proving and roundel-position proving are different evidence: a lamp can be illuminated while the colour-selection mechanism fails to reach its commanded position. A four-aspect searchlight arrangement adds a separate upper yellow to provide double yellow.
The lamp, reflector, roundel and lenses form the optical system. A reflector designed into that system must be understood with its associated controls and optical design, rather than applying a rule inferred from a different signal head. Main and auxiliary filament arrangements also have to maintain the intended optical alignment.

title: 7  Lineside signals
text:
7.8 Route indicators and signal sighting
A junction direction indicator, often called a feather or route arm, identifies a diverging route using an illuminated row of white lights. A theatre-type indicator displays a character identifying a route or destination. Their uses depend on visibility and operating context.
A route indication complements the signal aspect. It does not replace the need for the route to be correctly established. The controls must associate the indication with the route actually proved.
Physical signal design must make the intended display recognisable. Hoods, backgrounds, lens alignment and suppression of misleading reflections contribute to this. Plan symbols represent the signal’s function and orientation; the exact physical installation requires more information than the scheme-plan symbol alone.

Proving the route display
A junction indicator must produce a recognisable indication before the associated main aspect is permitted where route-display proving is required. A relay proving circuit can assess the selected lamp group through its designed current conditions. The number of lit lamps and their contribution to recognisability are equipment-specific.
A theatre-type display forms a character by illuminating selected lamp groups or an optical pattern. Some lamps are shared between different characters. Its controls must select the correct combination and obtain the required lamp-proving indication; finding current in any one lamp does not prove the intended character.
A stencil displays a fixed legend when illuminated. Alternative stencils need controls that prevent conflicting legends appearing together. Fibre-optic arrangements can carry light from a lamp to the positions that form the displayed pattern. The control path, light source, optical path and visible legend are distinct links in that chain.

title: 7  Lineside signals
text:
7.9 Shunt and subsidiary signals
Shunt signals authorise movements under a different set of conditions from a main running signal. A proceed shunt indication must not be assumed to prove the route clear to the same extent as a main running route. Some shunt movements are specifically intended to approach vehicles already standing on the line.
A subsidiary signal is associated with a main signal and can authorise a movement while the main aspect remains at danger. A call-on is a use that allows a train to enter an occupied line under the applicable conditions, such as entering a platform to join another train. The interlocking conditions are specific to the movement.
Other arrangements include preceding shunt signals, yellow shunts, opposing-locking-omitted arrangements and limit-of-shunt signals. These names identify specific purposes; they are not interchangeable variants of a universal shunting permission. In particular, a limit of shunt defines the limit of the relevant movement rather than providing a proceed aspect.

title: 7  Lineside signals
section: 7.10 Fitting a train into an occupied platform
text:
7.10 Fitting a train into an occupied platform
Lime Street control uses the occupation of defined approach and platform sections to establish whether an approaching train can fit into the available space. Its logic depends on the relative lengths and occupation of those sections, not merely on a generic “platform occupied” indication.
Suppose the available platform section and a designated approach section have equal lengths. If the approaching train is standing at the signal but also occupies a further section behind that approach section, it is too long for the assumed space. The call-on conditions therefore exclude that state.
This is an example of translating a physical requirement into train-detection conditions. It must be understood from the actual layout and control requirements before its logic can be interpreted.

title: 7  Lineside signals
text:
7.11 Automatic Warning System
AWS combines track equipment and trainborne equipment to provide an audible indication and a visual reminder. In a standard signal-associated arrangement, the train receiver encounters a permanent magnet with its south pole uppermost and then an electromagnet which presents the required north-pole field when energised.
The permanent magnet initiates the warning sequence. The subsequent energised electromagnet produces the clear indication under the required signal conditions. If that cancelling field is absent, the driver receives the warning and must acknowledge it; failure to acknowledge initiates a brake application.
The cab’s yellow-and-black sunflower or sunburst indication reminds the driver of an acknowledged warning. It is not a live repeat of the signal aspect: the signal can change after the train has passed the equipment. The driver still responds to the signals and route requirements.
For a permanent warning, such as a defined speed-restriction warning arrangement, a permanent magnet can be used without the signal-associated cancelling electromagnet. Bi-directional arrangements can require suppression and additional control of the magnetic fields so that the equipment has its intended effect for each direction.

The inductor circuit
A relay-controlled AWS electromagnet can include both the green aspect-control condition and lamp-proving condition in its feed. The circuit therefore needs more than an instruction to display green. Both feed and return paths and the specified proving conditions must be followed when interpreting it.
An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field. A suppression diode or rectifier across the coil limits the switching transient when the current is interrupted, reducing arcing at the controlling contacts in the arrangement concerned. Its polarity and circuit connections form part of the design.
The track mounting, protecting ramp, magnet identity, direction and relationship to the associated signal are also functional parts of the installation. Correct electrical operation alone does not establish correct positioning or mechanical clearance.

title: 7  Lineside signals
text:
7.12 Train Protection and Warning System
TPWS provides defined brake-intervention functions through track loops and trainborne equipment. Its overspeed sensor system (OSS) uses an arming and trigger sequence on the approach. The elapsed time between the two is related to the train’s speed and the loop separation.
In a simple timing model, passing the trigger while the onboard timing window is still active initiates an intervention. Greater separation gives a longer transit time at the same speed, so loop position is a functional part of the designed threshold. A train stop system (TSS) uses a closely spaced loop arrangement at the protected location to initiate the defined stop intervention when active.
The signalling interface controls the required active state and returns the specified fault or health information. An instruction to activate is different from evidence that the installation is functioning. A fault indication must be interpreted through the actual interface and its designed signalling response.
TPWS addresses specified locations and conditions; it does not guarantee that every train will stop before every possible conflict. Performance depends on the layout, approach conditions, equipment and train braking. Loop spacings, timing values, suppression and tests belong to the applicable design and equipment requirements.

title: 7  Lineside signals
text:
7.13 Key points

Clearing means becoming less restrictive, not necessarily showing green.
Warning distance must support stopping at the protected location.
Four-aspect signalling adds an earlier warning stage; capacity depends on the whole arrangement.
An overlap is protection, not movement authority.
Shunt and call-on routes have purpose-specific controls.
Aspect selection, filament monitoring, optical performance and lamp proving provide different evidence.
AWS warnings and TPWS interventions depend on defined track-to-train arrangements.

title: 8  Circuit reading
text:
8.1 Drawings communicate different kinds of information
A signalling circuit is both a logical arrangement and a physical network of equipment, wires and terminals. Reading it requires you to understand what the circuit is intended to do and how the actual connections achieve that function.
Three drawing types answer different questions:
A scheme plan generally uses one line for each track. A bonding drawing needs the individual rail paths. Neither can replace the circuit detail needed to identify a particular relay contact or cable termination.
A schematic explains a principle with reduced detail. A working wiring diagram also identifies the connections needed for the installation. Always establish what kind of drawing you are reading before deciding what information it proves.

title: 8  Circuit reading
text:
Drawing
Main question
Typical contents




Signalling or scheme plan
What equipment is provided, and where does it apply?
Tracks, signals, point identities, train-detection sections and operating directions


Circuit or wiring diagram
How are the electrical functions connected?
Contacts, coils, supplies, terminals, cable cores and sheet references


Bonding diagram
How are the individual rails electrically connected or separated?
Insulated joints, rail bonds, jumper connections and traction-return arrangements






Wiring layout and the written circuit
A wiring layout can group a relay’s coil and contacts together, making the apparatus and its connections recognisable. A written circuit distributes the symbols into convenient feed-to-return paths, with function names identifying parts that belong to the same apparatus. Both can describe the same electrical connections while looking quite different on the page.
Converting between them is an exercise in preserving connections. Retain each terminal identity and junction, then follow the complete paths. Rearranging the symbols for clarity must not introduce a join where wires merely cross, omit a branch or exchange two contact terminals.

title: 8  Circuit reading
section: 8.2 Start with the title block and index
text:
8.2 Start with the title block and index
The title block identifies the installation, drawing number, sheet and revision. An index helps locate related sheets. Read these before concentrating on the circuit: a familiar-looking drawing for a different installation or revision can give a convincing but incorrect account of the equipment in front of you.
Build a small map of the drawing set. Locate the equipment circuits, supply and looping sheets, cable information, and rack or location profiles. The diagram containing a relay coil is not necessarily the sheet containing every contact of that relay.

title: 8  Circuit reading
text:
8.3 Symbol, identity and termination
A circuit element has three layers of information:

Symbol: what kind of electrical item or contact is represented?
Identity: which item performs this function?
Termination: exactly where does the connection enter or leave it?

For example, AE TPR identifies a track repeater relay associated with track circuit AE. R1 and R2 may identify its coil connections in a particular arrangement. A contact labelled AE TPR A1-A2 belongs to that relay but represents a different pair of physical connections. The actual drawing determines the terminal designations; do not assume every relay uses the same coil pair.
The same equipment identity can occur many times because a relay has several contacts. Repeated identity does not mean that every symbol represents a separate relay.

Read the whole symbol
The contact mark alone may be insufficient. The associated armature symbol, position letters, terminal designations and any timing or polarity notation distinguish different kinds of contact operation. A special symbol or reference number can direct the reader to a drawing note that supplies an essential condition.
Read those notes before assigning a state. In particular, a polar contact marked normal or reverse must be interpreted through the relay’s specified operation and retention behaviour. The relay contact and polar-relay explanations develop these distinctions. A neutral relay’s simple up/down table cannot be applied to every symbol.

title: 8  Circuit reading
text:
8.4 Reading function names
The final letter commonly identifies the apparatus, while preceding letters describe its function. The equipment number or track reference associates it with the railway item.







Example
Interpretation




AE TR
Track relay for AE


AE TPR
Track repeater relay for AE


23 ECR
Lamp-proving relay associated with signal 23


23 HR / HHR / DR
Yellow, double-yellow and green aspect-control functions


345 NWKR / RWKR
Normal and reverse point-detection relays for points 345


345 NWKE / RWKE
Normal and reverse point-indication lamps for points 345


WM
Point motor function in the applicable naming convention


T/J
Transformer-rectifier designation



Letters have different meanings in different positions. An R can describe reverse or red within a name and identify a relay at its end. Parentheses or quotation marks can identify special functions. Use the drawing conventions and the relevant symbol and nomenclature reference rather than guessing an unfamiliar combination.
The relays chapter develops the relationship between coil state, front contacts and back contacts. A front contact is not automatically closed just because it is called normal in ordinary conversation.

title: 8  Circuit reading
text:
8.5 Supply labels and protection
Supply labels follow their own convention. In a drawing using the following labels:







Label
Meaning




B50
Positive side of the identified nominal 50 V d.c. supply


N50
Negative side of that supply


BX110
Feed side of the identified nominal 110 V a.c. supply


NX110
Return side of that a.c. supply


BN or BNX
An intermediate connection in the relevant supply arrangement


E
An earth connection where shown



The number states a nominal voltage designation, not a measured result. B50 and N50 are the two sides of one labelled supply; the labels do not mean that each conductor has that voltage to earth. In an earth-free circuit neither side should simply be treated as an earth return.
Fuse identity and rating are separate information. f007 3A, for example, identifies fuse 007 with a 3 A rating. The rating is a protective-device characteristic, not the normal current drawn by every circuit it supplies.

title: 8  Circuit reading
text:
8.6 Trace the whole path
Start at the identified feed and follow the path through protection, controls, the load and the return. At every contact, ask which relay or mechanism operates it and what state makes it conduct. At every continuation, follow the stated reference rather than assuming that the line ends there.
For a simplified repeater circuit, the path can be written as:
B50 → fuse → AE TR front contact → AE TPR coil → second AE TR front contact → N50.
Both contacts must be made for the repeater coil to receive current. The second contact controls the return side; it is not a second source of power. This is an example of double cutting. Removing either required contact path prevents energisation in the ideal circuit.






Figure 8.1: Reading a complete feed-to-return path. The boxes represent named circuit elements, not standard wiring symbols.



The drawn order across the page makes the path easy to follow, but a wire may physically pass through several terminal strips and a cable before reaching the next element. Logical proximity is not physical proximity.

title: 8  Circuit reading
text:
8.7 Series, parallel and branching paths
Contacts in series all have to conduct for that path to be complete. Parallel branches provide alternative paths. A branch can also divide a shared feed between different loads, each with its own controls and return.
Do not confuse an alternative path around a contact with a separate load fed from the same junction. In the first case either branch may energise one coil. In the second, one branch can feed a lamp while another feeds a relay, and their remaining conditions may differ.
A discrete circuit has its own complete feed-to-return path. Several discrete circuits may appear on one sheet. Shared supplies can be shown through positive looping and negative looping, with a separate looping sheet identifying the fuse, connections and destination sheets. A circuit shown without the whole busbar arrangement still depends on those supply connections.

title: 8  Circuit reading
text:
8.8 Follow the boundary between locations
Incoming and outgoing describe direction relative to a stated location. A control can leave the relay room for a point machine, while detection returns from the point equipment. A circuit that is outgoing at one housing is incoming at another.
Follow both sides of the circuit across the boundary. Record the location identity, terminal, cable identity, core and receiving terminal. A matching function name alone does not prove that you have found the correct conductor.
Interlinking cables connect equipment within a relay room or between racks and the operating equipment. An interface can therefore exist within a building as well as along the railway. A rack or location profile helps turn the electrical identity into a physical position.

title: 8  Circuit reading
text:
8.9 Red and green alteration work
Alteration drawings distinguish the existing arrangement from work to be added or recovered:

Red identifies new work or additions.
Green identifies work to be removed or recovered.
Black generally represents retained work, subject to the drawing’s stated conventions.

An all-new sheet can be endorsed accordingly, while a sheet being recovered can carry an overall recovery marking. Complex work can use separate addition and recovery drawings. Colours must be read with the issue, stage, notes and endorsements; a greyscale print can conceal important distinctions.
Adding a connection to a spare contact of an existing relay does not necessarily mean installing a new relay. Likewise, removing wires from a contact does not necessarily mean recovering the relay. The markings identify what changes, down to the relevant connection or item.






NoteRead an alteration as two arrangements



First establish the retained circuit with the green work removed. Then trace the completed circuit with the red work added. This helps expose a bypass, a missing return or an unintended change of logic without treating a coloured line as an isolated instruction.

title: 8  Circuit reading
section: 8.10 Worked example: following a missing indication
text:
8.10 Worked example: following a missing indication
An indication lamp is controlled by a point-detection repeater in a relay room. Its drawing refers to a separate looping sheet for the feed and to an interlinking cable for the lamp on the operating floor.
A learner looks only at the repeater contact and concludes that a closed contact proves the lamp should be lit. The conclusion omits the fuse and shared feed, the interlinking cores, lamp connections and return. It also assumes that the correct physical contact has been identified.
A complete account names the supply, fuse, controlling contact, intervening terminals, cable cores, lamp and return. If any part is uncertain, the explanation is incomplete. This is a drawing-reading exercise, not authority to disturb or test the operational circuit.

title: 8  Circuit reading
text:
8.11 Key points

Different drawings represent the railway, the logic and the individual rail or wire connections.
Identify the symbol, equipment function and terminals separately.
Trace the complete path, including shared supply sheets and returns.
Incoming and outgoing have meaning only relative to a location.
Red and green describe alterations; drawing status and stage determine how to interpret them.

title: 9  Relays and relay logic
text:
9.1 A switch operated by an electromagnet
A relay combines a coil, a magnetic circuit, a moving armature and electrical contacts. Coil current produces a magnetic force that moves the armature. The movement operates several contacts, allowing one circuit to influence other circuits without directly joining all their electrical supplies.
A relay is energised when its coil is supplied as required, and de-energised when it is not. In the ordinary neutral-relay example, it picks up when energised and drops away when the supply is removed. Special relays can have different behaviour, so the type matters.
The contact state is defined relative to the relay’s operated state:
The words front and back avoid the ambiguity of saying “normally open” when a relay may normally be kept energised in service. A track relay, for example, can be energised throughout the time its section is clear.
