Communication link
Carry detection-point information to the evaluator


ACE
Evaluate the information for the configured sections


Power Data Coupling Unit (PDCU), where used
Couple power and data onto the line pair, or provide the specified communication interface



The ACE includes processing, power-supply and input/output boards. In a two-out-of-two arrangement, two processing channels must produce the required agreement. Serial input/output receives detection-point information; parallel input/output provides section information. CAMTECH’s AZLM equipment description shows these equipment relationships.






Figure 10.2: Three detection points define two sections, with a shared boundary at D2. The lines below show information flow to the ACE, not a cable wiring arrangement.




From a wheel to a section state
The transmitter and receiver coils at the rail contact are magnetically coupled. A passing wheel changes the received signal. The two sensing positions provide a sequence from which wheel passage and direction can be established; the two channels must be interpreted together.
In AZLM, the trackside electronics carry out counting supervision and generate digital messages for the ACE. The ZP30H detection-point arrangement uses two independent microcontrollers, with supervision from the evaluator. Its communication uses coded telegrams over the specified link. A voltage present on the line pair alone cannot establish that valid count information is reaching the intended evaluator.
The ACE processes the received information through its vital computer system and produces occupancy information through the configured output interface. The detection point, message path, processing and output are distinct stages to account for when studying a failure. Network Rail’s AZLM description, Appendix B.3, sets out this architecture.


Worked example: a train crosses a shared boundary
In Figure 10.2, sections A and B are initially valid and clear. A train of 12 axles enters A at D1. The train then crosses D2 towards B. After five axles have passed D2, the teaching count is seven in A and five in B: both sections are occupied.
After all 12 axles have crossed D2, A can return to clear if all its validity conditions are satisfied; B still contains 12 axles. It can return to clear after the corresponding departures at D3 and the required valid processing. The shared detection point supports two different section balances. It does not make the two sections one continuous count store.


Read indications as evidence
Keep three questions separate: is the detection-point equipment functioning, is its information being received correctly, and what section state has the evaluator established? A healthy local indication does not, by itself, answer all three. Similarly, a group of affected sections can suggest a shared boundary, communication or supply dependency without proving which component is faulty.
Identify the installation, detection-point identities, associated sections, equipment versions and applicable diagnostic information. Record relevant indications and the circumstances before any authorised action that could clear retained evidence. Rail-head alignment, mounting, cables, electronics, communication and power belong to the complete detection chain. The cable and power-supply chapters explain the electrical paths without repeating their test principles here.


Resetting and restoration
A reset changes the evaluator’s counting or section state under its defined conditions. Restoration returns the detection function to operational use through the required controlled arrangements. Neither finding a physically empty-looking section nor obtaining a zero display establishes all the evidence needed for restoration.
The permitted reset method and its prerequisites depend on the installed system and application. Follow the relevant controlled instructions for AZLM; a plunger sequence, relay arrangement or reset inhibit from another axle-counter family cannot be assumed to apply. This chapter explains the distinction, rather than prescribing a reset or restoration sequence.

title: 10  Train detection
section: 10.15 A methodical account of a failure
text:
10.15 A methodical account of a failure
Begin with the expected state and the observed symptom. Establish the section identity, feed, receiver and any repeaters before explaining why the displayed state differs from expectation. A panel indication, local relay state and rail input are related evidence, but they refer to different points in the chain.
Group possible causes by function: energy generation, the feed path, rail continuity, unwanted shunts or leakage, receiver operation, and transmission of the resulting state. This keeps a missing indication from being treated automatically as a failed track relay. Compare the symptoms with shared supplies and recent work as well as with the individual circuit.
Record the conditions associated with observations, including weather and whether the symptom is intermittent. Measurements must be interpreted against the circuit type and authorised test arrangements. A structured explanation narrows the uncertainty; it does not justify raising the feed or bypassing a proving condition merely to obtain a clear indication.

title: 10  Train detection
section: 10.16 Worked example: an empty section shown occupied
text:
10.16 Worked example: an empty section shown occupied
A section appears physically empty but has no clear indication. Is that necessarily a wrong-side failure?
No. If loss of feed, a connection fault or invalid evaluator information removes the clear indication, the signalling system may correctly take the restrictive state. The physical observation and the equipment state are different evidence. The response should be interpreted from the system design, without treating appearance alone as authority to restore a clear indication.

title: 10  Train detection
text:
10.17 Key points

The basic track circuit requires positive energy for the clear indication.
Shunting and ballast leakage affect the electrical balance differently.
Feed regulation must preserve both the clear-state and occupied-state margins.
Rail configuration and bond layout determine the consequences of a disconnection.
Bonds, joints and traction return are integral to the design.
Detection used to prove clearance must account for the vehicle body beyond its wheelsets.
Axle counters depend on valid counting and system state.
AZLM separates trackside detection, digital communication, central evaluation and section outputs.
A restrictive output can represent a fault as well as a train.

title: 11  Interlocking
text:
11.1 From a command to a protected movement
Interlocking prevents incompatible routes, controls when points may move and determines when a signal may clear. It must maintain the required protection while a train approaches and traverses the route, and release it only under the specified conditions.
The entrance-exit interface simplifies entering the signaller’s route command. It does not collapse the engineering process into one event. Route commanded, route available, route locked and signal cleared describe different stages.

title: 11  Interlocking
text: Figure 11.1: A simplified route-setting and release lifecycle. Each transition is subject to its designed conditions.

title: 11  Interlocking
text:
11.2 Availability before movement
First establish that the commanded route exists and that its required points are available. A point already in the required position may be available; a point locked in the opposite position is not. The availability check prevents unnecessary point movements for a route that cannot be established.
The system then calls the required points and establishes route locking. Point detection supplies the required indications to the signal controls. Availability and detection answer different questions: “may this point be used as required?” and “is the required state proved?”

title: 11  Interlocking
text:
11.3 Route locking and conflicting movements
Route locking prevents the points being changed in a way that would destroy an established movement. Locking functions are associated with the successive train-detection sections of the route and overlap.
Some conflicting routes require a common point in opposite positions. Locking the point for the first route prevents availability for the second. Other conflicts cannot be excluded that way. In particular, opposing routes can use the same point positions while authorising trains towards one another. Directional route conditions must exclude that conflict.
White route indications and red occupation indications help the signaller follow the state. Their detailed meaning depends on the interface. They are information about the underlying functions, rather than the locking mechanism itself.

title: 11  Interlocking
text:
11.4 Conditions for clearing the signal
For an invented main route from S1 to S3 over points P1, consider the simplified requirement:
Route set and locked AND P1 detected reverse AND T1 clear AND T2 clear AND overlap O1 clear AND the required S3 proving satisfied.
Each item has a purpose:







Condition
What it establishes in this example




Route set and locked
The correct route exists and its required protection is established


P1 detected reverse
The required point state is proved


T1 and T2 clear
The route sections required clear are proved clear


O1 clear
The required overlap section is proved clear


S3 proving
The specified signal-in-advance proving is satisfied



This is a learning expression, not a complete control table. Flank conditions, aspect sequence, approach controls and other requirements can also apply. If any required term is false, the expression does not permit clearance.

title: 11  Interlocking
text:
11.5 Approach control and approach locking
These terms sound alike but serve different purposes.
Approach control regulates when a signal clears as the train approaches. For a junction with approach control from red, a signal is held at danger until an approach condition is satisfied so that the train has reduced speed before taking a divergence. Depending on the design, occupation, timing and aspect conditions can be involved.
Approach locking maintains route protection after a signal has been cleared and is then replaced. A driver may already have acted on the proceed aspect and may be unable to stop before the signal. Replacing it to danger does not mean that the route locking has released or that the route is immediately free to alter.
A release may depend on a look-back assessment, a timing condition, passage of the train or another designed sequence. No generic delay from an introductory example should be applied as a site instruction.

title: 11  Interlocking
text:
11.6 Train-operated cancellation and sectional release
Train Operated Route Release (TORR) uses a defined sequence of train-detection operations associated with passage of the train. One occupied input alone is insufficient: a detection failure could otherwise mimic the event used to cancel a route.
Cancellation and release must be distinguished. A route can be cancelled while locking remains in force. Once the release conditions are met, sectional release removes locking behind the train in the specified sequence. A section ahead of the train must not become available merely because a preceding section has cleared.
A simplified learning sequence is:

The signal clears with the route protected.
The train passes the signal and the signal is replaced.
A valid passage sequence cancels the route command where TORR is provided.
Locking releases progressively as the required sections clear behind the train.
Remaining overlap or other locking releases under its own specified conditions.

Different layouts need different release conditions. The governing requirements are recorded for the actual route.

title: 11  Interlocking
text:
11.7 Point locking has several causes







Type
Purpose




Route locking
Preserve an established route or protected arrangement


Dead locking
Prevent point movement when the associated train-detection section is occupied


Individual-control or key locking
Hold points in a selected position through the control arrangement


Time-of-operation locking
Address movement timing where a train could reach points before a newly initiated movement finishes



Dead locking and route locking can apply simultaneously. Waiting until the point section becomes occupied may be insufficient where the points are close to its boundary. Locking must address the train’s approach and the equipment’s movement time, rather than just its eventual position.

title: 11  Interlocking
text:
11.8 Flank protection
A route can need protection from equipment outside its direct line of travel. Points in a siding or on an adjacent connection may be positioned and locked to prevent an unwanted movement reaching the route. This is flank protection.
The precise detection indications required depend on the arrangement. Do not assume that every flank point has the same detection requirements as a point traversed by the train. Read the specified controls, including any additional track-clear conditions associated with alternative protection.

title: 11  Interlocking
text:
11.9 Overlaps and alternative paths
An overlap can include several sections and points. Trailing points can require a particular locked position. Facing points can provide alternative overlap paths if the design permits a swinging overlap.
A swinging overlap is a controlled change between valid protected arrangements. It does not mean that the points are unrestricted. Availability, detection, conflicts, timing and train occupation must all be addressed as required. Overlap release may also differ from route release, for example where a train stops at a platform and a later movement needs the points beyond it.

title: 11  Interlocking
text:
11.10 Shunt routes and ground frames
A shunt route may not require every section up to its destination to be clear, because the movement can be intended to approach standing vehicles. This does not make its point detection or route protection optional. Each movement has its own requirements.
A ground frame provides local control of a limited group of equipment. A release from the controlling signaller enables the local operation under the specified protective conditions. Restoring the frame and its equipment to the required state is part of handing control back. A release is an engineered interface between two control arrangements, not merely permission conveyed by an indication lamp.

title: 11  Interlocking
text:
11.11 Control tables
Control tables record the requirements for routes, points and other signalling functions. Signal-route entries include setting conditions, point and track proving, aspect controls, replacement, approach locking and train-operated release. Point entries describe movement restrictions, route locking, releases and overlap conditions.
Separate signal and point sheets organise the requirements by purpose. Start by identifying what a row or column governs, then relate each entry to the layout and the other tables. Do not infer a complete requirement from a fragment of circuit or software data.

title: 11  Interlocking
section: 11.12 Worked example: cancelled but still locked
text:
11.12 Worked example: cancelled but still locked
A signaller cancels a route just after a train has seen its proceed aspect. The signal returns to danger, but the points remain locked. Is the locking necessarily faulty?
No. Approach locking may be preserving the path for a train that cannot stop in time. If the train enters the route, its occupation and subsequent release sequence may continue to hold the necessary locking. The visible replacement of the signal is only one event in the complete process.

title: 11  Interlocking
text:
11.13 Key points

Availability, locking, detection and aspect control are different stages.
Opposing routes can conflict without requiring opposite point positions.
Approach control governs clearance; approach locking protects an approach after clearance.
Cancellation does not automatically release locking.
Control tables define the requirements for the actual arrangement.

title: 12  Solid State Interlocking
text:
12.1 What SSI means here
This chapter uses SSI for the British Rail-developed Solid State Interlocking system. It is a particular system architecture, not a name for every electronic interlocking.
SSI implements the interlocking functions introduced in the previous chapter using processors, application data and trackside interfaces. The change of technology does not remove the need to prove points, exclude conflicts and retain locking for a train.

title: 12  Solid State Interlocking
text:
12.2 The interlocking cubicle
The Multiprocessor Modules (MPMs) carry out the interlocking processing. Three modules compare their results and internal information. In the two-out-of-three arrangement, a disagreeing module can be isolated while the two agreeing modules continue. If the remaining pair disagree, continued safe agreement is no longer established and the system shuts down as designed.
This combines two purposes. Comparison supports the detection of an erroneous result. Having three modules also permits continued operation after one has been isolated. Three copies do not make the application data correct: all three could process the same incorrect requirement consistently. Safety therefore also depends on the program, data, engineering process and interfaces.







Item
Principal role




MPM
Interlocking processing and associated communications


Panel Processor Module (PPM)
Interface to the signaller’s control equipment


Diagnostic module
Monitor system behaviour and provide diagnostic information


Technician’s terminal
Display diagnostics and provide specified technician facilities


Data Link Module (DLM)
Interface to the relevant data-link path


Trackside Functional Module (TFM)
Interface between data telegrams and local railway equipment

title: 12  Solid State Interlocking
text:
12.3 Fixed program and application data
The fixed program provides the common processing functions. The application data defines the particular railway: equipment identities, route conditions, point controls, release sequences and other required relationships.
The distinction makes a reusable system possible, but application data remains safety-critical. It must represent the approved requirements accurately. Data preparation at a design workstation is followed by compilation and simulation before use. Successful compilation establishes that data can be translated; it does not prove that every railway requirement has been represented correctly.
A useful learning chain is layout and requirements → application data → compiled representation → tested behaviour. Each transition can introduce an error and needs the appropriate assurance.

title: 12  Solid State Interlocking
text:
12.4 The signaller and technician interfaces
The PPM links SSI with a hard panel or electronic control interface. The PPMs are duplicated for availability. That is different from the triplicated interlocking comparison function. A control interface commands actions; the interlocking remains responsible for enforcing its conditions.
The technician’s terminal and recording facilities make internal state and events accessible. Time-related records help reconstruct the order of commands, occupation changes, detection changes and outputs. Their interpretation depends on what was actually recorded, its timing and the corresponding equipment indications.
Specified technician controls can impose additional restrictions, such as holding a signal at danger. They do not provide a general means of bypassing normal interlocking conditions. Use of those facilities requires the relevant authority and instructions.

title: 12  Solid State Interlocking
text:
12.5 Trackside functional modules
A TFM receives a control telegram and returns indication information. The SSI trackside arrangement supports addresses 1-63 on a trackside system, with actual capacity and spare allowance considered in the scheme design. Addresses identify which module a telegram concerns; the correct association between address, wiring and application data is essential.
Duplicated internal channels within a TFM compare their operation. If agreement is lost, the module is taken out of service as designed. This is distinct from the three-MPM arrangement and has a different effect on availability: a TFM affects its associated functions, while failure of the central interlocking can affect the whole area.

Signal module
The signal TFM provides controlled outputs and indication inputs. Outputs can drive appropriate signal loads and other specified equipment. Current-sensing paths return evidence about the connected loads. Input circuits include checking intended to distinguish valid locally supplied input information from a spurious voltage.
Red retaining is a special arrangement supporting the most restrictive aspect when a module is disabled in the specified way. It depends on the designed circuit and available power. It is not a claim that every loss of a TFM or supply must leave a visible red.


Points module
The points TFM is designed around the outputs and inputs needed for point operation and detection. Its direct outputs suit clamp-lock equipment. Electric machines require the specified relay interfaces. A shared word such as “output” does not imply that every load can be connected directly.

title: 12  Solid State Interlocking
text:
12.6 Data links and long-distance interfaces
Duplicated trackside data links carry controls and indications. DLMs interface the electrical paths. Repeaters extend the supported baseband arrangement within its design limits. For longer transport through a telecommunications bearer, Long Distance Terminals (LDTs) provide the required interface.
An internal data link provides communication between interlockings. Do not confuse that boundary information with the trackside link to TFMs or the panel interface to the signaller.
Duplicating the links improves availability only to the extent that common failures have been addressed. Two paths in one vulnerable cable route can both be lost together. The physical routing and the equipment shared by them therefore matter as well as their logical names.

title: 12  Solid State Interlocking
text:
12.7 Other electronic interlockings
Other electronic interlockings, including Ebilock, VPI and WESTRACE, implement electronic safety in different ways. These include comparison of diverse processing, coded or checked logical processing and checked input/output architectures. The general lesson is that a system’s safety case cannot be inferred from the number of processors alone.
Equipment-specific architecture, diagnostics and permitted actions must be learnt for the actual system. SSI terminology should not be assumed to describe another manufacturer’s modules directly.

title: 12  Solid State Interlocking
section: 12.8 Worked example: duplication and a cable cut
text:
12.8 Worked example: duplication and a cable cut
A and B links are both working, but they pass through the same damaged section of route. Both fail together. Why has duplication not preserved communication?
The paths were logically separate but shared a physical failure exposure. Availability depends on independence from the failures being considered, not merely on providing two interfaces. Route diversity and common equipment must be considered together.

title: 12  Solid State Interlocking
text:
12.9 Key points

SSI implements signalling requirements using processing, data and local interfaces.
Processor agreement and correct application data are separate requirements.
Duplication and triplication serve defined safety and availability purposes.
TFMs translate between telegrams and local equipment.
Diagnostics provide evidence; they do not replace the complete system documentation.

title: 13  Remote control systems
text:
13.1 Why transmit many functions together?
Providing a dedicated pair of long-distance wires for every control and indication becomes costly as an area grows. Consider 200 controls and 500 indications over 30 km. At two conductors per function, that is 1,400 conductors and 42,000 conductor-kilometres.
Conductor-kilometres describe the total length of individual conductors. They do not mean that the cable route is 42,000 km long. The route remains 30 km in the example. Keeping those quantities distinct makes the engineering and cost argument clear.
Multiplexing shares a transmission path between functions. The functions remain identifiable by a rule, such as an allocated time slot or frequency channel.

title: 13  Remote control systems
text:
13.2 Time Division Multiplex
In Time Division Multiplex (TDM), each function occupies an allocated part of a repeated sequence. Imagine matched switches at the sending and receiving ends stepping through inputs and outputs in the same order. Input 1 is conveyed to output 1, then input 2 to output 2, and so on. The rotating switches are an analogy; the equipment performs the function electronically.
Synchronisation keeps the two ends aligned. If alignment is lost, the receiver must not simply treat one function’s information as another’s without the system’s defined response.
A panel-to-interlocking TDM system carries signaller controls to a satellite relay interlocking and brings indications back. The local interlocking enforces its safety conditions. This allows the control transmission to have a different safety role from a direct vital proving circuit.






ImportantLocate the safety boundary



A remote route command and a vital point-detection input are different kinds of information. Whether a transmission path must itself be vital depends on the function and the complete architecture. Panel-to-interlocking TDM can be non-vital because the interlocking checks the commands. That does not make all signalling transmissions non-vital.

title: 13  Remote control systems
text:
13.3 Reconstructing indications
An indication that flashes at the panel need not be transmitted as a series of timed on/off samples. A scan could distort that pattern. The system can send state information such as “flashing required” or “steady required”, then generating the actual presentation locally.
This separates the information from its display. A panel processor can reconstruct several indications from the transmitted state, reducing the number of transmitted functions. The display must still be associated with the correct equipment and have a defined response to lost or invalid information.

title: 13  Remote control systems
text:
13.4 Frequency Division Multiplex
In Frequency Division Multiplex (FDM), functions share the pair by using different frequency channels. Function A can transmit at frequency f1, B at f2 and C at f3. A receiver for A responds to the intended f1 signal and controls its associated follower relay.








Feature
TDM example
FDM example




How a function is distinguished
Position in a timed sequence
Allocated frequency channel


Main coordination need
Synchronisation and correct message association
Stable generation, selective reception and compatible channel allocation


Typical application
Block transfer between control centre and satellite interlocking
Collection or distribution of trackside functions



Several frequencies can be present together on the pair. Their separation must be engineered: filtering, harmonics, interference and equipment faults matter. “Different frequencies” alone is not a complete argument for independence.

title: 13  Remote control systems
text:
13.5 Reed equipment
A reed is a mechanical resonator whose vibration is determined by its physical properties. A reed filter uses two reed assemblies on a coupled frame. An incoming electrical signal drives one reed; mechanical vibration is transferred to the other; its coil provides an electrical output when the intended resonance is established.
In the receiver, this selective transfer supports acceptance of the assigned frequency. In the transmitter, the reed filter forms part of the oscillator’s frequency-control arrangement. The intended result is a stable, recognisable channel rather than a frequency that can drift into another function’s channel.
Reed equipment has separate filter and electronic units, coding to prevent incorrect substitution, and follower relays matched to the receiver. Vital and non-vital versions have different roles. Physical similarity is not sufficient evidence that equipment has the required frequency, safety role or output characteristics.

title: 13  Remote control systems
section: 13.6 The line is part of the system
text:
13.6 The line is part of the system
The transmitter’s connection must not interrupt every other function when one unit is removed. The line arrangement retains continuity, with receivers connected across the pair. Line levels and impedance also affect the whole circuit.
Amplifiers maintain signal level where required. In a vital frequency-based arrangement, they must preserve the characteristics on which safe recognition depends. Isolation addresses electrical conditions along the railway, including induction from traction. Equipment selection and positioning follow the actual design, rather than a generic distance rule.
A simplex path carries information in one direction. A half-duplex path uses both directions at different times. A full-duplex path supports both directions simultaneously. These terms describe direction and timing of communication, not whether the signalling function is safe.

title: 13  Remote control systems
section: 13.7 Worked example: identical symptoms from a shared path
text:
13.7 Worked example: identical symptoms from a shared path
Six distributed indications disappear together. Each has its own local source contact, but all use one FDM pair and a common receiving supply. What does the pattern suggest?
It identifies shared dependencies worth comparing with the system records: the line pair, common power, amplification or receiving equipment. It does not prove which item failed. Independent local faults remain possible, but a simultaneous group change is evidence about the system structure.
The useful reasoning step is to map the affected functions to what they share before interpreting each as an unrelated equipment failure.

title: 13  Remote control systems
text:
13.8 Key points

Multiplexing reduces dedicated transmission wiring by sharing a path.
TDM separates functions in time; FDM separates them by frequency.
Safety requirements depend on the function carried and its place in the architecture.
Reed systems rely on controlled resonance and selective reception.
Shared line and power arrangements can produce groups of symptoms.

title: 14  Telecommunications
text:
14.1 Services and bearers
Telecommunications carries voice and data between the people and equipment operating the railway. A useful distinction is between a service, such as a signaller-driver call or an SSI data connection, and its bearer, such as a copper circuit, optical transmission path or radio link.
Several services may share a bearer. A service can also use more than one bearer to improve availability. To understand a failure, identify both the user-facing function and the infrastructure that carries it.
Telecommunications includes lineside telephones, concentrators, SSI links, transmission systems, passenger information and radio. Their equipment differs, but common questions recur: who is connected, how is the circuit identified, what information is carried, what delay is acceptable, and what happens when a path fails?

title: 14  Telecommunications
text:
14.2 Lineside telephones
A signal post telephone (SPT) provides a direct connection associated with a particular signal and controlling location. Other direct lines serve level crossings, adjacent control locations and operational interfaces. Dial telephones provide access to a telephone network, while maintenance plug points support communications between staff at equipment locations.
Identity is essential. The person answering must know the circuit involved, and the caller must identify their location and purpose through the applicable communication arrangements. A technically clear voice path to the wrong person or location does not meet the operational need.
Outdoor telephones also need suitable environmental protection, labels and physical robustness. Their lines and housings are part of the service, alongside the switching equipment at the control centre.

title: 14  Telecommunications
text:
14.3 Telephone concentrators
A concentrator brings many dedicated operational circuits to the signaller’s console. Its functions include circuit identity, controlled call selection, prevention of unintended overhearing or interruption, and clear indication of which caller is connected.
Call parking lets a caller remain associated with the system while the signaller deals with another call. It is different from joining callers together. Distinctive indications identify urgent or special calls. Recording provides evidence of communications, with the associated need to preserve the relevant record when required.
The engineering objective is more than making speech audible. A dependable operational service must deliver speech to the intended party and make its identity unambiguous.

title: 14  Telecommunications
text:
14.4 Diverse routing
If adjacent lineside phones all depend on the same vulnerable cable path, one cut can remove several means of communication together. Alternating route directions and transmission paths can reduce the effect of a single fault on neighbouring facilities.
Diversity must be assessed physically. Separate circuit numbers do not prove separate cables, ducts, power supplies or transmission nodes. The same point applies to duplicated signalling data links.
Remote concentrators can combine low-use local circuits before sending them over a longer path. This reduces dedicated long-distance wiring while preserving the required call-control functions. The network arrangement must still address power, identity, capacity and failure behaviour.

title: 14  Telecommunications
text:
14.5 SSI long-distance links
An SSI baseband link uses the appropriate DLM interfaces and trackside cabling. An LDT adapts it for transport through a telecommunications bearer, with a corresponding interface at the remote end.
The bearer must meet the signalling service’s requirements, including timing. A path can be electrically intact and carry data, yet fail the service if delay or the relative arrival of duplicated messages is outside the permitted limits.
For learning, separate four checks:

Continuity: is a path available?
Integrity: is the required information correctly conveyed?
Timing: does it arrive within the specified constraints?
Independence: what failures can affect both A and B paths?

The permitted delay and message-timing limits depend on the SSI/LDT arrangement. They must be established from the applicable interface and design documentation.

title: 14  Telecommunications
text:
14.6 Digital bearer allocation
Digital transmission equipment can carry several operational voice and signalling data services over one bearer. PCM channel and aggregate interface rates describe available transmission capacity; the circuit allocation and interface records establish which service reaches which destination.
For a signalling link, identify its allocated channel, end interfaces and required timing and integrity. A healthy aggregate bearer or a familiar interface rate does not establish that the correct signalling service is connected end to end. This is particularly important after transmission alterations or a change of route.

title: 14  Telecommunications
text:
14.7 Multiplexing and transmission hierarchy
TDM shares transmission capacity through timed channel positions. Transmission systems include Plesiochronous Digital Hierarchy (PDH), with tributary clocks operating within tolerances, and Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SDH), with a coordinated timing structure supporting access to channels at intermediate nodes.
A drop-and-insert point lets channels be taken from or added to a transmission system without terminating the entire service path. Digital regeneration reconstructs a valid signal at a stage, rather than simply amplifying everything present, including noise. It still depends on a receivable input and a correctly operating system.
An optical fibre carries signals as light and removes a conductive connection along that fibre. It does not remove the need for powered terminal equipment, correctly engineered interfaces and a resilient physical route.

title: 14  Telecommunications
text:
14.8 Passenger information and radio
Customer information systems include public address, recorded announcements, displays and clocks. Automatic updates depend on the correct association between service information, location and time.
Radio provides a mobile communications path. Coverage, selective calling, emergency calls and association between a train and the relevant control area are important radio-system functions. These are examples of system functions, rather than an inventory of equipment at a particular site.
Voice communications, a data bearer and the safety system using that data are distinct functions. Radio coverage alone does not establish a safe movement authority. The complete train-control arrangement must define and assure that authority and its supervision.

title: 14  Telecommunications
text:
14.9 Worked example: connected but unusable
Both ends of a signalling data service report a connection, but valid messages are rejected after a transmission route change. Why is “the link is up” insufficient evidence that the service is satisfactory?
Connection status says little about the message integrity, latency or relationship between duplicated paths. A new route can change those characteristics. The service must be assessed against its end-to-end requirements, using the evidence and responsibilities defined for that interface.

title: 14  Telecommunications
text:
14.10 Key points

Services and bearers are different layers of the system.
Operational speech needs correct identity as well as audibility.
Route diversity addresses common physical failures.
Data services can have strict timing as well as continuity requirements.
Channel allocation and interface records connect a signalling service to its bearer.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.1 Start with the load
Signalling equipment needs energy as well as control information. A relay coil, a signal lamp and a point motor have different voltage, current and duty requirements. A supply must suit its connected load and remain adequate during the conditions for which the installation is designed.
A continuously energised relay imposes a steady demand. A point movement imposes a relatively large intermittent demand. A signal can change which lamp is energised while continuing to require a dependable supply. These patterns influence the choice of supply, protection, distribution and standby arrangements.
The main devices introduced here perform different jobs:
A transformer-rectifier can supply d.c. equipment or form part of a charging system. Those functions do not make every transformer-rectifier a complete battery charger.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
Device
Main function




Cell or battery
Produce electrical energy through chemical action


Transformer
Transfer a.c. energy between windings and provide the designed voltage ratio and isolation


Rectifier
Convert a.c. into unidirectional current


Charger
Supply the controlled charging conditions needed by a rechargeable battery


Distribution and protection
Convey energy to the loads and control the consequences of faults

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.2 Batteries in signalling supplies
A rechargeable signalling battery provides reserve when its normal supply is unavailable and, in some arrangements, supports intermittent equipment demands. Establish the battery type, nominal voltage, cell arrangement, charger and loads from the supply records. The way the cells or strings are connected affects the available voltage, capacity and charging requirements.
Battery identity matters when interpreting readings or selecting replacement equipment. A series string depends on every cell and intercell connection; a weak cell or resistive connection can limit the performance of the complete supply. Where parallel strings are provided, their intended current sharing and protection are part of the design.

Primary cells: background
A primary cell supplies energy through a chemical reaction that is not intended to be reversed by charging; once exhausted it is replaced. Zinc-carbon dry cells and wet primary types have been used in signalling where a local self-contained supply was needed. They are useful background knowledge for interpreting older drawings, but the practical battery coverage in this book concentrates on rechargeable supplies.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.3 Battery voltage under signalling load
A satisfactory unloaded voltage does not prove that a battery can support its signalling duty. Internal resistance, cell condition and intercell connections can produce a marked voltage fall during a point movement or other demand. Distinguish a fall at the battery terminals from the additional drop between the battery and the equipment.
Record the load condition with the voltage. A reading taken while the battery is on charge, supplying its ordinary relay load or supporting a point movement describes a different condition. Compare the evidence with the applicable battery and equipment requirements.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.4 Standby capacity and discharge rate
The stated Ah capacity must be read with its rated discharge conditions and end voltage. The important signalling question is whether the battery can maintain its defined loads for the required standby period, including any intermittent demands. Temperature, age, state of charge and discharge rate affect usable reserve.
A battery can cease to support a relay, lamp or point machine before all its nominal capacity has been used, because the equipment’s minimum input condition has been reached. Capacity, charger indication and open-circuit voltage are therefore different evidence about supply performance.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.5 Lead-acid cells
A lead-acid secondary cell has positive and negative plates separated within an acid-resistant container. Its electrolyte is dilute sulphuric acid. The chemical condition of the plates and electrolyte changes as the cell charges and discharges.
For accessible flooded cells, electrolyte specific gravity (SG) can provide evidence of charge state when interpreted with the cell type, temperature and condition. A hydrometer measures liquid density relative to water; SG is dimensionless, not a voltage reading. Designs with sealed or otherwise inaccessible electrolyte require their own assessment methods.
Prolonged discharge can allow persistent sulphation to develop, reducing usable capacity and increasing internal resistance. A battery’s condition therefore cannot be established solely from its external appearance or the charger being switched on.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.6 Rechargeable alkaline cells
Rechargeable alkaline cells use an alkaline electrolyte, commonly potassium hydroxide in the types considered here. Their construction, voltage characteristics and charging requirements differ from lead-acid cells. Nickel-cadmium and nickel-iron identify different electrode systems and must not be treated as interchangeable names.
Electrolyte specific gravity does not track state of charge in the same way as in a lead-acid cell. A familiar hydrometer reading must therefore not be given the same interpretation across different chemistries. Battery identity is essential before interpreting test results or selecting charging equipment.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.7 Charging arrangements
Initial charging prepares a cell or battery for service where its supply condition requires it. Recharging restores charge after discharge. Neither has a universal current or duration applicable to all batteries.
A trickle-charging arrangement supplies a relatively small charging current, associated with replenishing charge between intermittent demands. The average load and charging capability must be compatible; a short operating cycle can create a high peak demand while drawing relatively little average current.
A float-charging arrangement maintains the battery at its specified standby charging condition while the supply supports the normal load. On loss of the normal supply, the battery can support the circuit for its designed duty. Correct voltage control and current capability remain necessary.
A regulated constant-voltage charger holds the designed output characteristic while its current changes with battery and load conditions, within its rating. Constant voltage does not mean constant charging current or unlimited output current.
Undercharging leaves insufficient reserve and can damage some chemistries. Excessive charging can cause heating, electrolyte loss and gas evolution. The charging system must match the battery, its application and the manufacturer’s requirements.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.8 Local transformers
Signalling distribution can use a higher a.c. voltage with local transformers providing the supplies needed by lamps, track circuits and other equipment. Identify the primary supply, secondary circuit, rating and selected tapping from the actual installation. Conversion, isolation and the condition of the downstream circuit must all be accounted for.
Transformer tappings provide the designed output choices. Selecting a different tapping is not a general remedy for low voltage at equipment: first distinguish the transformer output from voltage lost in cables, contacts and terminations. A satisfactory no-load secondary voltage does not establish that the circuit remains adequate under its signalling load.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.9 Isolation and earth-free circuits
Isolation can separate a signalling supply from the earthing arrangement of its upstream source. In an earth-free circuit, an unintended connection to earth can remain hidden until another fault creates an unwanted path. The circuit’s protective and monitoring arrangements are therefore part of the supply system.
An isolating transformer does not make every downstream part harmless to touch. A voltage still exists between its output conductors, and other sources or induced voltages can be present. The actual circuit and isolation arrangements govern the work.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.10 Transformer-rectifiers
A signalling transformer-rectifier combines local voltage conversion with a d.c. output for its specified equipment. Establish whether the installation also provides smoothing, regulation or battery charging; those functions cannot be assumed from a transformer-rectifier label.






Figure 15.1: Voltage conversion, rectification and any smoothing or regulation are distinct stages.



A missing or defective stage can produce different symptoms: no output, low output, excessive ripple or inadequate performance under load. A label stating d.c. does not mean that the output has no ripple, and a correct no-load reading does not prove rated load capability.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.11 Follow the distribution path
A typical study path is incoming supply → distribution and protection → local conversion → local protection → cable and terminals → load → return. Add the battery and charger paths where provided. Identify which supplies and indications are shared by several items.
A signal transformer can have input voltage while its lamp circuit remains incomplete. Conversely, low voltage at a load can result from cable or terminal resistance rather than the power unit. The cables chapter explains that distinction further.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.12 Alternative supplies and changeover
A second incoming supply and a local standby generator provide different forms of resilience. Two incoming feeders can still share an upstream dependency. A generator has its own dependencies, including starting energy, fuel, control equipment and the changeover path. Counting the available sources is therefore only the start of understanding supply security.
Changeover equipment transfers the load between the intended sources. The interval before the alternative supply is established matters: a generator cannot be assumed to deliver immediately after the normal supply disappears. A battery-backed circuit can bridge an interruption only within its designed capability. Follow which loads actually receive that support, rather than assuming that every load at a site is battery backed.
Supply indications must also be interpreted separately. An indication that a feeder is available is different from evidence that the load has transferred to it and is receiving the correct voltage. Source condition, changeover position and load condition answer different questions.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.13 Distribution arrangements
A radial or linear feeder supplies successive locations along a path. A fault or isolation near its source can affect several downstream locations. A spur branches from a main distribution path to serve a particular load or group. The location of the branch and its protection determine how much equipment shares a dependency.
A ring arrangement offers paths around a loop, subject to its designed switching and operating state. An open conductor can be masked by the other path, while equipment believed disconnected from one direction may still have another feed. Recognising a loop on a drawing does not establish where it is open, how it is protected or which sources can energise it.
The supply diagram should therefore be read as a network. Mark the sources, changeover devices, section boundaries, protection, conversion equipment and loads. This reveals both the extent of a supply failure and the possible sources remaining during an isolation.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.14 Fuses and discrimination
A fuse is designed to interrupt excessive current according to its characteristic. Its ampere rating is not an exact instantaneous operating threshold. The magnitude and duration of fault current, fuse type and prospective fault conditions affect its operation.
Discrimination means coordinating protective devices so that the device intended to clear a fault operates while supplies to unaffected circuits remain available. For example, a fault beyond a local branch fuse should, within the designed conditions, be cleared there rather than remove a whole feeder through its upstream protection. Merely fitting progressively larger ampere ratings towards the source does not establish that coordination; operating characteristics matter too.
An incorrect replacement can alter both protection and discrimination. The specified type and rating must be preserved. A higher rating is not a remedy for repeated operation: the fault or unsuitable operating condition still needs to be established through the authorised work arrangements.

Worked example: several locations lose supply
A local circuit fault occurs at the third location on a teaching radial feeder. The upstream feeder protection operates and all five locations lose supply. This differs from the intended selective response in which only the affected branch would be disconnected.
The observation directs attention to the fault path, the protective devices and their coordination. It does not prove that the upstream device is faulty: the actual fault current, downstream device, connections and specified characteristics all need to be understood.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
section: 15.15 Worked example: voltage falls during a point movement
text:
15.15 Worked example: voltage falls during a point movement
An invented battery-fed circuit has 24 V at the battery terminals but only 20 V across the motor during a demand of 8 A. The 4 V difference occurs in the complete connecting path, giving an equivalent resistance of \(4/8 = 0.5\) ohm at that moment. Its power loss is \(8^2 \times 0.5 = 32\) W.
The arithmetic does not identify the faulty connection. It shows why the battery terminal reading alone cannot establish the motor’s supply conditions. If the battery terminals also fell markedly during demand, battery internal resistance or charging condition would be additional possibilities. The complete set of measurements and circuit conditions would be needed.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.16 Equipment condition and practical boundaries
Study the significance of damaged containers, leakage, corrosion, loose or overheated terminals, electrolyte condition where accessible, and charger indications. Chemical hazards and stored electrical energy exist even when the mains input is disconnected. Batteries can deliver high fault currents at relatively low voltage.
Practical inspection, isolation, loading, electrolyte handling and charging require the relevant equipment instructions, electrical safety arrangements and competence. The examples here explain the relationships; they do not prescribe a charging current, test load or acceptance limit.

title: 15  Signalling power supplies
text:
15.17 Key points

A supply has to suit the load’s voltage, current and duty cycle.
Battery type, cell arrangement and charging must suit the defined signalling duty.
Internal and connection resistance matter especially under load.
Capacity in Ah is conditional and does not itself guarantee standby duration.
Transformers, rectifiers, chargers and distribution each perform different functions.
Alternative supplies depend on a working changeover path; protection coordination limits the extent of a fault.

title: 16  Signalling cables
text:
16.1 A cable is part of the circuit
Cables join the elements shown on a circuit diagram. They carry controls to equipment, indications back to the interlocking or display, and power to the loads. A cable fault can remove a required function or create an unintended path between functions.
An individual cable can contain circuits with different purposes. Losing several indications together can therefore point towards a shared cable, termination or supply. It does not prove that all the associated trackside items failed independently.

title: 16  Signalling cables
text:
16.2 What is inside a cable?
The conductor carries current and is commonly copper. A core is an individual insulated conductor within the cable. Its insulation electrically separates it from other cores and surroundings. The sheath protects the assembly from its environment; additional armour or other layers are included where specified.







Part
Main concern




Conductor
Resistance, current capacity and mechanical integrity


Core insulation
Separation between the individual electrical paths


Sheath
Protection against moisture, contamination and physical damage


Armour, screen or other specified layer
The mechanical or electrical function defined by the cable design



A sound-looking sheath does not prove that every conductor is intact. Conversely, visible sheath damage does not describe the full extent of the internal damage. Strand construction affects flexibility, while conductor area, insulation, installation conditions and protection all influence the permissible duty.

title: 16  Signalling cables
text:
16.3 Cable families and their roles
Lineside cables connect the interlocking area and trackside locations, or connect locations along the railway. Multicore arrangements can carry several controls or indications together. Some cores can be designated spare for future use or approved changes.
Tail cables connect a local housing to equipment such as signals, points, AWS apparatus or rails. They occupy an exposed part of the installation and have to accommodate the actual route and equipment interface. Track-circuit tail length and electrical characteristics can be part of the equipment design.
Power cables distribute the energy required by the equipment. A signalling distribution arrangement can use 650 V a.c. with local conversion, but the actual voltage and circuit must be established from the installation. Power cables must not be assumed to have unused spare cores.
Interlinking cables connect racks, rooms or operating equipment. Being within a building does not remove the need to identify their cores, terminal positions and circuit functions correctly.
Cable type, core count and appearance help recognition but do not prove identity. Use the markings and records associated with the actual cable.

title: 16  Signalling cables
text:
16.4 Core numbering and cable ends
Core numbers let the same conductor be identified at each termination. In a concentric multicore numbering arrangement, numbering progresses through layers outwards from the centre. Viewed into the cut face, the progression runs clockwise at the A end and anticlockwise at the Z end.
The ends present opposite views of the same laid-up cable. This convention helps interpretation, but it is not a substitute for reading the core identification. Different constructions can have different identification arrangements, so the applicable cable information must be used.
A core number, terminal number and wire-function identity are different things. Core 7 can connect terminal 12 at one location to terminal 18 at another. The record must preserve that relationship rather than silently treating all three numbers as equivalent.

title: 16  Signalling cables
text:
16.5 Voltage drop in signalling circuits
A point motor can impose a much larger current demand than an indication circuit. Resistance in the outgoing core, return core, contacts and terminations can therefore have different effects on the two functions. An indication that works with little current does not prove that the complete path can support the motor demand.
For a remote relay or signal lamp, compare the supply and load conditions through the complete path. A resistive termination can reduce the equipment voltage and heat under load while leaving apparent continuity. The point-movement example applies these relationships to a signalling load.

title: 16  Signalling cables
text:
16.6 Routing and the mechanical environment
Cable routes can include troughing, buried sections, ducts and undertrack crossings. Tail cables pass into equipment housings through their designed entries and glands. Protection, support and allowance for movement matter at transitions between these arrangements.
Think about the path as well as the endpoints. A cable can be affected by tamping, excavation, sharp edges, unsecured lids, water, heat or equipment movement. Mechanical work near points and rail connections can affect both the cable and the equipment’s reference position.
The circuit-reading chapter explains how to follow a circuit across location boundaries. Combine that electrical route with the physical cable route when studying an installation.

title: 16  Signalling cables
text:
16.7 Recognising damage







Observation
Possible significance




Cuts, abrasion or exposed inner layers
Loss of physical protection or insulation damage


Crushing, flattening or sharp distortion
Damaged conductors, insulation or both


Discolouration, melting or scorching
Heating from an electrical fault or an external source


Hardening, cracking or splitting
Deterioration of the sheath or insulation


Oil, chemical residue or other contamination
Possible material degradation and a handling hazard


Gnawing or disturbed protection
Animal damage that can extend beneath the visible surface


Corrosion or overheated terminals
Increased connection resistance or moisture-related damage



Observation gives evidence; disturbing a suspect cable can change the fault or worsen its condition. Inspection and any handling must follow the work arrangements rather than treating a visible defect as permission to disconnect it.

title: 16  Signalling cables
section: 16.8 Continuity, identity and insulation answer different questions
text:
16.8 Continuity, identity and insulation answer different questions
A continuity test examines whether the intended conductor provides an unbroken electrical path. Identification establishes that the path is the intended core and terminates where the records require. Insulation resistance testing examines unwanted leakage between conductors or from a conductor to earth.






Figure 16.1: Continuity concerns the intended path; insulation concerns unwanted paths away from it.



A conductor can have good continuity and poor insulation at the same time. A cross-connected pair can also conduct perfectly while sending the function to the wrong terminal. A satisfactory result in one category cannot stand in for the others.

Understanding a loop continuity measurement
On a disconnected teaching cable, two cores linked at the remote end make a loop that can be measured from one end. Its resistance includes both conductors, the temporary link and the test connections. A good loop reading alone does not separate the resistance of each core.
A reference core can support comparison with other cores, but its own identity and integrity first have to be established. Otherwise a fault in the reference can make several healthy cores appear faulty. Parallel paths through connected equipment can also give misleading apparent continuity.
This explains the test principle. The actual connections, isolation, instruments and sequence are defined by the authorised test arrangements.


Understanding insulation evidence
Core-to-core insulation concerns separation between functions. Core-to-earth insulation concerns separation from the reference earth and surrounding conductive paths. The two results are not interchangeable.
Insulation resistance is affected by cable length, moisture, temperature and contamination, as well as the condition of the material. Compare records only when their units and relevant conditions are understood. Do not confuse a low resistance required along a conductor with the high resistance required through its insulation.
An insulation test applies its own voltage. Equipment connected to the cable can affect the result or be damaged by an unsuitable test. Instrument settings, selection of cores, treatment of connected equipment and acceptance criteria therefore come from the applicable instructions.

title: 16  Signalling cables
text:
16.9 Installation, periodic checks and restoration
Initial testing establishes the required evidence for a newly installed or replaced cable. Periodic testing provides evidence about deterioration during service. A previous satisfactory result does not prove that no damage has occurred since it was recorded.
Spare cores can be included in defined monitoring arrangements, but their results cannot establish the condition of every working core. The specified maintenance regime determines which observations and tests are required.
A job is not complete merely because a test reading is satisfactory. Terminal identity, restored connections, removal and accounting of temporary links, protection and the required functional tests all belong to the complete work and testing arrangements.

title: 16  Signalling cables
section: 16.10 Worked example: continuity without correct operation
text:
16.10 Worked example: continuity without correct operation
A six-core teaching cable has core 4 broken and cores 5 and 6 transposed at the far end. A simple end-to-end check finds continuity on the conductors serving terminals 5 and 6, and the learner declares those connections correct.
The conclusion confuses continuity with identity. The paths conduct, but each reaches the wrong terminal. A test arrangement that proves the association between each end is needed to reveal the transposition. The break on core 4 is a separate fault; finding it does not prove that the other cores are correctly connected or adequately insulated.

title: 16  Signalling cables
text:
16.11 Key points

A cable carries defined functions through identified conductors and terminals.
Conductor integrity and insulation integrity are different requirements.
The complete loop determines voltage drop; a high-resistance connection can heat under load.
Core numbering must be related to the actual termination records.
Testing includes correct preparation and restoration, as well as obtaining readings.

title: 17  Useful other sources of information
text:
17.1 OFFICIAL DOCUMENTATION
Different resources answer different questions: how equipment works, what a task requires, what applies at a location, or what a technical term means. The following are useful starting points for study and day-to-day reference.
crumbs: 17  Useful other sources of information

title: 17  Useful other sources of information
text:
Signal maintenance specifications (SMS)
The Signal Maintenance Specifications describe the maintenance tasks and technical requirements for signalling equipment. Use the applicable specification to establish what must be inspected, maintained or measured, together with the relevant limits and recording requirements.


Signal maintenance testing handbook (SMTH)
The Signal Maintenance Testing Handbook sets out the processes, checks and tests for signalling maintenance testing within its defined scope. It helps establish the testing required after work such as equipment replacement, together with the associated planning and records.


Network Rail standards
Network Rail standards set out requirements for engineering, maintenance, safety and the management of railway assets. Use the controlled standards system to check the applicable document, issue and compliance date.


RSSB rulebook
The RSSB Rule Book contains the operational rules, modules and handbooks relevant to railway roles. For an S&T technician, it explains responsibilities and arrangements for working on signalling equipment and communicating with those controlling train movements.


Sectional Appendix
The Sectional Appendix provides route-specific information, including track layouts, line names, mileages, permissible speeds and local instructions. It is useful for understanding the railway at a particular location and relating equipment to its operational setting.


Hazard Directory
The National Hazard Directory records known hazards and location information to support planning and working on Network Rail infrastructure. Consult the relevant entries alongside the site-specific information and arrangements for the work.


Course notes
Course notes provide explanations, diagrams and worked examples from formal training, making them useful for revision and refreshing equipment knowledge. Check any task requirements or numerical limits against the applicable controlled documentation.


Network Rail e-learning
Network Rail e-learning provides online learning modules and assessments to support training, briefings and revision. Use the modules relevant to your role to prepare for courses or revisit topics that need further study.


eB suite
The eB suite is used to store, manage and retrieve engineering documents and records, including drawings. Check the document identity, revision and status to establish that the record is appropriate for the equipment and work being considered.
